sources.news_title: Trump orders Lake Ontario to be renamed ‘Lake America’
sources.text:
Trump stepped up his trolling of Canada by signing an executive order changing the name of the body of water on the border between the North American neighbours.
But Canadian prime minister Mark Carney swiftly rejected Trump’s move, saying it would be called Lake Ontario “then, now and always.”
The volatile US leader’s move comes after US-Canada trade talks collapsed at the last minute last week, prompting the two longtime allies to slap tit-for-tat tariffs on each other.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” the 80-year-old Republican told journalists as he signed the order at the White House.
Asked by an AFP reporter why he was targeting an ally for punishment instead of America’s adversaries, Trump replied: “The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people.”
Behind Trump’s desk in the Oval Office were two maps – one with the words “Lake America” in red over the lake, and the other with the header, “Making the Great Lakes Even Greater.”
Canada strikes back
Lake Ontario is the smallest by surface area of the five Great Lakes, which straddle the border between the United States and Canada. It borders the Canadian province of Ontario and the US state of New York.
The name change mirrors Trump’s unilateral altering of the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in January 2025 – a move Mexico has also rejected.
Carney retorted that the name of the lake was 400 years old – predating the formation of both the United States and Canada – and came from an Indigenous word meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”
“We know that America is changing,” he said in a post on X.
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Carney’s defiance of Trump in recent days has won plaudits at home.
In Toronto, Canada’s largest city which lies on the lake’s northwestern shore, Canadians and Americans alike criticised Trump’s move.
“Typical Trump. He’s being a bully, he goads, he antagonises,” said Mark Weicker, who lives in Kitchener, west of Toronto.
“He’s just trying to egg us on,” chimed in Jake Marchuk, who was visiting from Alberta province.
Megan Smith, who hails from New Jersey, put it bluntly: “It just makes him look stupid.”
‘All we need is an ocean’
Trump’s executive order tells the US department of the interior to update references to the lake in the official geographical naming service within 30 days and ensure the federal government calls it “Lake America.”
It justifies the name change by saying that the deepest part of the lake is on the American side, meaning that the United States “claims most of the Lake’s volume.”
Trump – who faces low approval ratings amid the Iran war and economic woes at home, with crucial US midterm elections around the corner in November – said he had been thinking about the name change “for a long time.”
The US president even hinted at renaming oceans that border the United States.
“We have a gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both,” he said.
During his second presidential term, Trump has irked a series of allies with his outlandish territorial claims, including that Canada should become the 51st US state.
Trump has also laid claim to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Nato ally Denmark, and talked about making Venezuela a state following the US capture of its leader Nicolas Maduro.
In recent days, he has also said that he will make the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman a US territory, despite the fact that the war with Tehran remains ongoing.

sources.news_title: Trump signs order renaming Lake Ontario 'Lake America'
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump announced Thursday that Lake Ontario will be known as “Lake America" within the United States, making the change as tensions with Canada escalate over trade, according to The Associated Press.
Trump signed an executive order at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office instructing the Interior Department to update the lake's name in the US geographic naming system. The order gives the department 30 days to implement the change, despite Trump's assertion that it was “official, effective immediately."
Trump said he had “notified all of the various people that we have to notify. So, we’ve done everything that you have to do."
The president has promoted the renaming idea in recent days as Washington and Ottawa have imposed retaliatory tariffs on one another. The US announced 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after trade negotiations collapsed. Canada responded with tariffs on $20 billion in US products, including steel, dairy goods, appliances and agricultural equipment.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Canada since returning to the White House last year and has suggested that the country become the 51st US state.
During the signing ceremony, a map of the Great Lakes displayed behind Trump labeled Lake Ontario as “Lake America" in large red letters. A second map carried the message, “MAKING THE GREAT LAKES EVEN GREATER."
Trump said his decision was not intended to convey a specific geopolitical message, but argued that “Canada’s been ripping us off for a long time" over trade and military matters.
“They wanted to be treated like a state and they’re not a state," the president said. “We just can’t do that anymore."
“We love the people of Canada," Trump added. “I don’t think their representatives do, an appropriate job. Maybe they’ll change. I really don’t know. It doesn’t make much difference."
Canadian officials quickly dismissed the move. Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston wrote on social media, “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy."
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has repeatedly clashed with Trump, dismissed the proposed renaming earlier this week as “a lot of rhetoric."
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded in a post on social media, writing, “The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big"."
“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America," added Carney.
“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario - then, now and always," concluded the Prime Minister.
Trump's latest renaming effort follows his decision last year to change the US government's designation of the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America."
After signing the order and holding it up for photographers, Trump said, “And we filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else."
He also suggested that additional bodies of water could eventually be renamed.
“So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean," Trump said. “So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them."

sources.news_title: Trump’s latest renaming effort turns Lake Ontario into ‘Lake America’
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has signed an executive order directing the U.S. government to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” escalating an increasingly tense dispute with Canada.
CNN reported Thursday that Trump signed the order in the Oval Office, where large maps of the Great Lakes were displayed behind him. Trump said the change was “effective immediately” and claimed his administration had completed the necessary paperwork.
The White House order directs the Interior Department and the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to update federal geographic records within 30 days. The Geographic Names Information System is also to be changed to remove federal references to Lake Ontario and replace them with Lake America.
Trump framed the decision against the backdrop of his deteriorating relationship with Canada. In remarks reported by CNN, he accused Canadian officials of treating the United States badly and described Canada as difficult to deal with on trade.
The president also suggested the renaming campaign could extend beyond the lake. According to CNN, Trump joked that after changing the names of a gulf and a lake, the administration might eventually consider renaming the Atlantic or Pacific oceans.
The White House order offers a more detailed explanation for the decision. It argues that the lake is an important American economic, commercial and defense resource and says the United States has invested heavily in protecting the Great Lakes. The order also claims the deepest parts of the lake are within U.S. territory.
But the move does not give Washington the power to dictate what Canada calls the lake. Lake Ontario borders New York and the Canadian province of Ontario, and the U.S. order specifically concerns federal government references and geographic records. Other governments and international bodies are not automatically required to adopt the new name.
The announcement follows Trump’s earlier attempt to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, another move that became part of his broader effort to reshape official geographic naming.
For now, Lake Ontario remains the name widely used outside the U.S. federal government, while American federal agencies begin implementing Trump’s preferred name, Lake America.

The order gives the department and the U.S. Board on Geographic Names 30 days to complete the changes.
The name change applies to U.S. government usage. It does not require Canada or other countries to adopt “Lake America.”
Canadian officials have said they will continue to refer to the body of water as Lake Ontario.

sources.news_title: Why “Lake America” isn’t funny
sources.text:
This story appeared in The Logoff, a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here.
Why “Lake America” isn’t funny
Trump’s lake stunt, briefly explained.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump says he’s renaming Lake Ontario. Let’s talk about it.
Can he really do that? Probably, though it doesn’t mean anyone will listen.
Strictly speaking, Trump’s executive order, signed Thursday in the Oval Office, directs the Interior Department to update the lake’s name to “Lake America” in the US’s Geographic Names Information System. It remains to be seen whether products like Apple and Google maps will follow suit, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, whose state contains the US portion of the lake, says she won’t.
Why is he doing that? The immediate answer is that Trump launched a trade war with Canada over the weekend, and he’s mad that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney won’t give him what he wants; this is a petty way to lash out.
That doesn’t explain the trade war itself, though. Unfortunately, when my colleague, noted Canadian resident Zack Beauchamp, went looking earlier this week, he couldn’t find an explanation either. As he writes, there’s absolutely no constituency for this fight — other than Trump’s own imperial desires as he keeps joking-but-maybe-not-joking about making Canada the 51st state.
Isn’t this just a stupid stunt? It’s a stupid stunt — but not just that. As my colleague Caitlin Dewey wrote earlier this week and Zack can attest, Canadians are royally pissed at the US. The trade war might feel like one more Trump fit of pique to Americans, but for Canadians, it’s a serious threat.
Thursday’s executive order further ratchets up those tensions, and it specifically plays into the (very credible) school of thought that Trump isn’t really in this to redress US-Canada trade imbalances; as with many things Trump, it’s about dominance and the desire to claim a “win” at any cost.
Lastly, it’s worth dwelling for a second on the stunt itself. One, Lake Ontario isn’t Canada’s name for it; it predates either country. And two, ad hoc renaming of bodies of water — this isn’t even the first time this Trump term — puts Trump in some fairly uncomfortable company.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
My colleague Sara Herschander just debuted her new newsletter, Nice Things, which feels like a great fit for this section. It’s all about dreaming big to build a better America, one with widespread high-speed rail, affordable housing, and infrastructure that works. You can subscribe here and read a story from the first edition here.
Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you back here tomorrow!

sources.text:
Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday he is renaming Lake Ontario to be known as “Lake America” in the United States as he escalates his trade war with Canada.
The Republican president signed an executive order directing the Interior Department to update the lake’s name in the U.S. geographic naming service. Trump cannot force Canada to follow along, however.
Trump has been floating the idea of the name change in recent days as the U.S. announced it was imposing 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down. Trump has been needling America’s northern neighbor since he returned to the White House last year, suggesting the ally with whom the U.S. once had warm relations should instead be absorbed as the 51st state.
Canada responded to Trump’s import taxes this week by imposing retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion worth of American goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment.
Trump, who signed the order as he was sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, had a large sign behind him propped on a stand with a map of the Great Lakes. Over Lake Ontario, in big red letters, the map read “Lake America.”
On the other side of the president was another map with the words, “MAKING THE GREAT LAKES EVEN GREATER.”
Trump said as he was signing the order that he’d “notified all of the various people that we have to notify. So, we’ve done everything that you have to do.”
“And this is official, effective immediately,” he added.
But the executive order Trump signed shows that the changes are supposed to be made within 30 days.
Canadian officials dismissed Trump’s move.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, invoking the lake’s Indigenous roots and noting that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence.
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always,” he wrote.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has traded insults with Trump, said on X: “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.”
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said, “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy.”
The lake is one of multiple Great Lakes that the U.S. and Canada share borders along. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat whose state shares a border on the lake, wrote on X in response to the White House’s announcement that, “New York won’t be calling it that.”
There is no single international body that determines names of international bodies of water and Trump has wide latitude over how the U.S. government recognizes geographic places and landmarks.
The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which means “lake of shining waters.” The province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
Trump said that while his action was not meant to send any particular geopolitical message, “Canada’s been ripping us off for a long time” on trade and military issues.
“They wanted to be treated like a state and they’re not a state,” the president said. “We just can’t do that anymore.”
“We love the people of Canada,” Trump added. “I don’t think their representatives do, an appropriate job. Maybe they’ll change. I really don’t know. It doesn’t make much difference.”
The move is reminiscent of his move last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.”
Trump scribbled his name with a Sharpie pen on the executive order, then held it up for the cameras, offering, “And we filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else.”
He also suggested his push to rename bodies of water may not be finished.
“So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean,” Trump said. “So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them.”
Associated Press writer Rob Gillies in Toronto contributed to this report.

sources.text:
The trade war President Trump started with Canada seems to be preoccupying him far more than the actual war he started in Iran. That was apparent on Thursday, when he made good on perhaps the silliest threat he has directed toward American’s onetime close ally. As reporters looked on in the Oval Office, Trump signed an executive order to change Lake Ontario’s name to “Lake America” with the new name displayed on a map behind him.
The executive order directs Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, in conjunction with the Board on Geographic Names, to “take all appropriate actions” to officially rename Lake Ontario, including updating the Geographic Names Information System to remove all references to its original name and swap it to “Lake America.” Under the order, Burgum has 30 days from its signing to put these changes into action.
Trump’s move is reminiscent of his highly contested push last year to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico, the oceanic basin that neighbors the U.S. Gulf Coast as well as Mexico, to the “Gulf of America,” an unexpected change the president first floated in his inaugural address. He signed an executive order directing the change last January. Similarly, Trump moved to restore the name Mount McKinley to the Alaskan peak Denali, overturning an Obama-era renaming of the mountain to a moniker frequently used by Alaska’s Indigenous communities.
The president alluded to his penchant for changing storied names during his announcement and suggested he wasn’t finished. “If you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean,” he said. “Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific.”
In his statement denouncing Trump’s move, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney invoked the origin of Lake Ontario’s name, saying that it comes from “the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.’
“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” Carney said.
Congressional Democrats quickly denounced the change as proof Trump has the wrong priorities. “Sad and pathetic,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wrote on X. “Unable to solve a single problem facing Americans, this is what Trump resorts to. Voters will respond accordingly in November.”
Connecticut senator Chris Murphy had similar criticism. “This is why your gas and grocery prices are so high. Because he spends all his time on this bs,” he wrote.
Predictably, some Republicans appeared ready to embrace the change. Tony Wied, a Wisconsin congressman, expressed openness to additional Great Lakes name changes. “While we’re at it – Lake Wisconsin sounds good too,” he wrote.
Though Burgum has indicated he will follow through with Trump’s order, it remains to be seen who else will adopt the “Lake America” name. While federal agencies as well as services like Google Maps and Apple Maps adopted the administration’s “Gulf of America” change due to the GNIS updating the name within its system, the body of water’s original name is still widely used outside of the country.

Washington DC [US] August 28 (ANI): US President Donald Trump has signed an Executive Order directing that the body of water currently known as Lake Ontario be officially renamed "Lake America", amid an escalating trade war with neighbouring Canada.
The order, signed at the White House on Thursday (local time), directed the US Secretary of the Interior, in coordination with the Board on Geographic Names, to take appropriate action within 30 days to rename the lake and update the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).
"The body of water currently known as Lake Ontario is a tremendous asset to the United States and part of our Nation's heritage," the Executive Order stated
It further stated that the lake "has long been an integral asset to American exploration, settlement, commerce, and defense," citing its role in American trade, military logistics, shipping, manufacturing, agriculture and energy supply chains.
"In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation's economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America," the order stated.
The Executive Order also stated that "The United States is the greatest protector of the Great Lakes, including the body of water currently known as Lake Ontario."
"Without the security and investment provided by the United States, this freshwater system would not be open for shipping, recreation, and responsible use to the same extent as it is today," it stated.
The order said the United States Coast Guard supplies "9 of the 11 ice breaking vessels on the Great Lakes" and that the United States has invested nearly USD 4 billion in protecting the Great Lakes freshwater ecosystem over the last decade, while Canada has invested "far less" in similar initiatives over the same period.
The order also highlighted the lake's role in the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway system, stating that maritime commerce supports "hundreds of thousands of American jobs and billions of dollars in annual economic output, cargo value, and related business revenue."
Within 30 days of the order, the Secretary of the Interior, in coordination with the Board on Geographic Names, is directed to take appropriate actions to rename the body of water as "Lake America", bounded on the south and east by New York State and on the north, west and southwest by the Canadian province of Ontario.
The order further directed the Geographic Names Information System to be updated to reflect the renaming and remove references to Lake Ontario, consistent with applicable law. Federal government references to Lake Ontario, including on maps, contracts and other documents and communications, are also to reflect the new name.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the signing, Trump linked the move to his earlier renaming of the Gulf of Mexico.
"As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it and now it's very routinely the Gulf of America. So if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake, now all we need is an ocean. So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific, maybe we'll change them both," Trump said.
Trump also criticised Canada and Canadian officials, saying, "The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They're nasty people. They charge our farmers 400% tariffs. They've been doing it for a long time."
"And I had them figured out in my first term, and I did some pretty strong things and had it getting pretty good. And then the election was rigged, and now I'm coming back and doing it the way it... and finishing the job," he added.
"But they treat us very badly. Canada treats us very badly. I would say that of all countries, as you know, we have President Xi coming in a couple of weeks. Uh, we have a lot; we deal with a lot of people. People, oftentimes, they'll ask me, 'Who's the worst to deal with on trade?' And I said, 'That's easy, Canada.' They are the worst to trade, and they, they feel entitled, and just, we can't have that," Trump said.
The signing comes days after Trump first floated the proposal. On August 25, Trump said he was considering renaming Lake Ontario "Lake America", linking the proposal to US-Canada trade relations.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said, "The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don't expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer."
The body of water forms part of the five Great Lakes of North America and serves as a natural border between Ontario and New York State.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford had earlier dismissed Trump's proposal as "a lot of rhetoric" while highlighting Ontario's economic importance to the United States.
"I think it's a lot of rhetoric because we're the No. 1 customer to 17 states, No. 2 to 12 others. Ontario alone, if Ontario was just standalone, would be the third-largest trading partner in the world," Ford told CNN.
On August 25, Canada announced dollar-for-dollar, rate-for-rate counter-tariffs on US goods in response to Washington's decision to impose a 50 per cent tariff on USD 27.6 billion of Canadian goods, according to the Department of Finance Canada news release.
The escalation followed the United States imposing 50 per cent tariffs on roughly USD 20 billion worth of Canadian imports after the trade talks failed, with the measures affecting around five per cent of Canada's exports to the United States. (ANI)

US President Trump signs order renaming Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’
The rebrand comes as the US and Canada engage in a cross-border trade war after Trump increased tariffs last week.
Amid a spiraling trade war with Canada, United States President Donald Trump says he is renaming a body of water shared between the two countries.
At a Thursday news conference in the Oval Office, Trump signed an executive order that changes the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America. The president told reporters the name change will take place “effective immediately”.

When asked what message he was trying to send Canada with the renaming, Trump criticised the country’s trade relationship with US, claiming it “has been ripping us off for a long time”.
“Well, they haven’t treated us well. The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people,” Trump said.
“So the lake change – the Lake of America – was something I’ve been thinking about for a long time, actually.”
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has been embroiled in a renewed trade dispute with the US, dismissed the president’s order in a post on social media.
“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” Carney wrote on X. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Trump’s executive order comes days after negotiations between the two countries fell apart, which occurred hours before the August 22 deadline to avoid 50-percent tariffs on $20bn worth of Canadian goods.
Canada has responded with retaliatory measures, taxing roughly 700 US products valued at roughly the same amount.
Thursday’s order is not the first time Trump has renamed a geographical feature since the start of his second term.
Upon returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump signed an executive order that rebranded the “Gulf of Mexico” as the “Gulf of America”.
In the order, Trump justified the name change by stating the gulf “has long been an integral asset to our once burgeoning Nation and has remained an indelible part of America”.
However, cartographers and governments have used “Gulf of Mexico” for nearly 500 years, long before the US officially became a country.
Despite sharing a name with Canada’s most populous province, Lake Ontario took its official designation from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatari:io”, which translates to “lake of shining waters”. The province, founded in 1867, took its name from the body of water.
In the same 2025 order that renamed the Gulf of Mexico, Trump also reversed a decision by former President Barack Obama that changed the federal name of the state of Alaska’s Mount McKinley to Denali, which is how Indigenous people in the area have historically referred to North America’s highest peak.
Trump said he switched back the mountain’s name to honour the 25th US president, William McKinley.
Critics of the renaming trend, including some within his own Republican Party, were quick to condemn Thursday’s executive order.
“With all the challenges facing our country, this is what the President chooses to spend his time doing today and communicating to the American people and the rest of the world,” former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie wrote on X. “Childish. Completely childish.”
Others, like Trump’s former deputy press secretary Sarah Matthews, were even more candid.
“I bet this goes so f***ing hard if you’re stupid,” Matthews said.
Despite the criticism, Thursday’s order is largely symbolic and does not compel Canada to comply. It only affects how the US federal government refers to the name.
Mexico, for instance, does not recognize Trump’s “Gulf of America” rebranding, nor do many other countries and international groups. However, companies like the tech giant Alphabet, the maker of the widely-used app Google Maps, observed the order for users who perform searches within the US.
Trump’s name change policy has also been a source of friction between the president and news outlets. Last year, Trump sought to bar The Associated Press news agency from certain White House events over its use of the term “Gulf of Mexico”.
During Thursday’s Oval Office signing, Trump teased possible America-themed name changes for other bodies of water bordering the US.
“We have a gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean,” Trump said. “So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”

sources.news_title: Trump Signs Order Renaming Lake Ontario ‘Lake America’ For U.S. Agencies
sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” for official United States government use, escalating a symbolic dispute with Canada amid a widening trade fight.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters during the August 27 Oval Office signing. The White House followed with a similar post on X:
EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY: Lake Ontario is renamed to LAKE AMERICA! 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/ZFww8PexiW
— The White House (@WhiteHouse) August 27, 2026
The change applies to federal maps, databases, contracts, documents and agency communications. It does not require Canada, international organizations, private mapmakers or other countries to adopt the new name.
The order comes after trade negotiations between Washington and Ottawa collapsed and the United States imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods. Canada has announced retaliatory tariffs on an equivalent value of American imports.
Order Directs Federal Name Change
The executive order, titled “Honoring the American History of the Great Lakes and Renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America,” directs Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to work with the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to complete the change within 30 days.
The Interior Department must update the Geographic Names Information System, the federal government’s official database of domestic geographic names, and remove references to Lake Ontario from that system.
The Board on Geographic Names must also instruct federal agencies to use “Lake America” on government maps, contracts and other documents and communications.
The order says the United States has played a leading role in protecting and maintaining the Great Lakes. It notes that the U.S. Coast Guard operates nine of the 11 icebreaking vessels serving the lakes and says the United States has invested nearly $4 billion in the freshwater ecosystem over the past decade.
It also asserts that the deepest portions of Lake Ontario lie within U.S. territory and that the United States therefore holds most of the lake’s water volume.
Lake Ontario is shared by New York and the Canadian province of Ontario. Approximately 52% of its surface area lies on the Canadian side, according to Reuters.
An American executive order cannot compel Canada to use the new designation.
“We’ll always call it Lake Ontario. Period,” Canadian Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said before Trump signed the order, as USA Today reported.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded similarly Thursday.
“He can change it to whatever he wants,” Ford said in a statement provided to ABC News. “But it will always be Lake Ontario to all Canadians and the rest of the world!”
A Name Older Than Both Countries
The name Ontario predates both the United States and modern Canada. It is derived from an Indigenous Iroquoian term commonly interpreted as “lake of shining waters,” according to the Center for Great Lakes Literacy.
European maps were using versions of Lake Ontario by the 17th century. The Canadian province established in 1867 subsequently took its name from the lake.
Lake Ontario is the smallest of the five Great Lakes by surface area, covering approximately 7,340 square miles. It is about 193 miles long and 53 miles wide, according to figures cited by the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.
Toronto and several other major Canadian population centers sit along its northern and western shoreline, while Rochester, Oswego and other New York communities lie along the American side.
Trade Fight Preceded Renaming
Trump first publicly floated the new designation on August 25 after trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed. In a Truth Social post, Trump said the United States was giving “serious consideration” to the change because it did not expect to conduct much business with Ontario.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he suspended negotiations after the United States introduced last-minute demands affecting Canada’s other trading relationships, automobile sector, culture and French-language protections.
“As a result, last evening, I suspended trade negotiations with the U.S.,” Carney said in an August 22 address.
Washington has disputed Canada’s account and accused Ottawa of retreating from previously negotiated terms.
Canada subsequently announced counter-tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on products covering 27.6 billion Canadian dollars in U.S. imports. The measures are scheduled to take effect September 8, according to the Canadian government’s Department of Finance.
Trump Points To Gulf Precedent
The Lake America order follows Trump’s January 20, 2025, executive order directing federal agencies to use “Gulf of America” instead of Gulf of Mexico and restoring Mount McKinley as the federal name for Denali.
Mexico rejected the Gulf of America designation. Google Maps later displayed different labels based on a user’s location: “Gulf of America” in the United States, “Gulf of Mexico” in Mexico and both names elsewhere, the Associated Press reported.
Trump suggested Thursday that other geographic renamings might follow.
“We have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean,” Trump said, before mentioning the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, according to ABC News.
For now, Lake America is the required name within the U.S. federal government. North of the border, Canadian officials say Lake Ontario is not going anywhere.

sources.news_title: Republicans are already tired of Trump’s “petty” renaming of Lake Ontario
sources.text:
Vermont Gov. Phil Scott (R) on Thursday called President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America “petty and disappointing.”
“This is petty and disappointing. We should be at the negotiating table, finding a path forward that strengthens both the U.S. and Canadian economies,” wrote Scott in a Thursday social media post about the order. “Further escalating tensions does nothing to help American or Canadian families and businesses.”
          
Related
Trump’s order directs the Interior Department to update the lake’s name to “Lake America” in the US’s Geographic Names Information System. But it remains to be seen whether major media outlets and map service providers like Google and Apple will rename the lake. (Neither has renamed the lake as of Thursday evening.) New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) has also said she will not use the new name.
Trump’s renaming of the lake is part of a trade war that he launched against Canada over the weekend. Trump imposed a 50% tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian exports, including auto parts, forestry products, furniture, textiles, whiskey, and hockey equipment, economic professor Kent Jones wrote. Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney responded with a list of $20 billion in US imports that Canada will impose tariffs of up to 50% on — many of the tariffs will affect US industries in northern swing states bordering Canada.
    Never Miss a Beat
Subscribe to our newsletter to stay ahead of the latest LGBTQ+ political news and insights.
The trade war expands upon Trump’s repeated insults to the US’ northern neighbor: He has repeatedly referred to Canada as the 51st state (a reference that suggests possible invasion and annexation), and gay Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has voiced support for the Canadian province of Alberta to declare its independence from Canada.
Scott wasn’t the only Republican to disapprove of Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario.
“As long as I’ve been alive it’s always been Lake Ontario, and I see no reason why we should change it now,” said Rob Corradino, the Republican mayor of Oswego, a town where 62% of 2024 voters chose Trump, AL.com reported.
“From what I see, the Canadians are very strong-willed people, and they don’t take kindly to threats,” he added. “I think it’s best to get along with your neighbors. I would hope we could all get along for the betterment of both sides.”

sources.news_title: Trump orders Lake Ontario to be renamed Lake America
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump stepped up an escalating feud with Canada on Thursday, ordering that Lake Ontario – a body of water shared by both countries—be renamed “Lake America.”
Trump signed an executive order on the name change at the White House, further trolling Canada as the North American neighbours plunge deeper into a trade war.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
Behind Trump’s desk were two maps of the US-Canada border — one with the words “Lake America” in red over the lake, and the other with the header “Making the Great Lakes Even Greater.”
Asked why he was targeting an ally for punishment instead of America’s adversaries, Trump replied: “The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people.”
“People, oftentimes, they’ll ask me who’s the worst to deal with on trade? And I said that’s easy. Canada. They are the worst to trade with,” the 80-year-old Republican added.
Canada did not immediately comment but is unlikely to accept the renaming of Lake Ontario, the smallest of the five Great Lakes by surface area, which borders Canada’s Ontario province and New York state.
US-Canada trade talks collapsed at the eleventh hour last week, with Trump’s tariffs taking effect on Saturday.
Canada responded with tit-for-tat tariffs on Tuesday, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying: “You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked.”
The same day, Trump announced that he was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name to Lake America.
He then posted a TikTok video late Wednesday saying that he intended to do so after all.
‘Now all we need is an ocean’
The name change mirrors Trump’s unilateral altering of the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on his first day back in office in January 2025.
That change obliged the US federal government to refer to the gulf by the new designation, although Mexico has rejected any move to rename it and it lacks international recognition.
Trump said the name change was “something I’ve been thinking about for a long time, actually. As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it, and now it’s very routinely the Gulf of America.”
Trump also hinted at renaming oceans that border the United States.
“So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both,” he said.
While Lake Ontario shares its name with the Canadian province, the name itself is derived from the indigenous Huron word “Ontari’io,” which means “great lake” or “beautiful water,” according to the National Museum of the Great Lakes.
Toronto, Canada’s largest city, sits on its northwestern shore.
During his second presidential term, Trump has irked a series of allies with his outlandish territorial claims, including that Canada should become the 51st US state.
Trump has also laid claim to Greenland, an autonomous territory of NATO ally Denmark, and talked about making Venezuela a state following the US capture of its leader Nicolas Maduro.
In recent days, he has also said that he will make the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman a US territory, despite the fact that the war with Tehran remains ongoing.
AFP

sources.news_title: Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario ‘Lake America’
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C., Aug. 27, 2026 (Gephardt Daily) — Pres. Donald Trump on Thursday signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.
The executive order comes days after Trump floated the idea of a name change while speaking to reporters about failed tariff negotiations between the U.S. and its neighbor to the north.
“Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!,” Trump posted on social media Saturday. “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!”
Trump’s remarks came after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa would impose retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. after the Trump administration’s 50% tariffs on Canada took effect.
Carney told a press conference that his government would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”
Both nations have imposed the tariffs, as stated.
Ottawa, Canada’s capitol, is in the province of Ontario. Lake Ontario, named in 1660 by the cartographer Francis Creuxius, is bordered by Ontario on the north, west and southwest, and by the U.S. State of New York on the south and east.
Image: Google Maps
Trump made the announcement Thursday while standing in front of a graphic map of the Great Lakes region labeled “Make the Great Lakes Even Greater.”
CNN conducted an interview with Patrick Brown, mayor of Brampton, Ontario, to get his reaction.
“Well, we’re still going to call it Lake Ontario,” Brown said, smiling.
“I think many of you will still call it Lake Ontario, and the only person who’s going to have a trouble with what to call it is your president. That the whole notion is a bit preposterous, and just like if our prime minister wanted to rename the Mississippi, you’d probably get a chuckle out of it.
“It’s having the same reaction in Canada.”
The executive order signed by Trump is titled: “HONORING THE AMERICAN HISTORY OF THE GREAT LAKES AND RENAMING LAKE ONTARIO AS LAKE AMERICA.”
The text is below:
By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered:
Section 1. Purpose and Policy. As I announced in Executive Order 14172 of January 20, 2025 (Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness), it is the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements. The United States is the greatest protector of the Great Lakes, including the body of water currently known as Lake Ontario. Without the security and investment provided by the United States, this freshwater system would not be open for shipping, recreation, and responsible use to the same extent as it is today. The United States Coast Guard supplies 9 of the 11 ice breaking vessels on the Great Lakes, securing commercial shipping lanes free of charge. The United States has invested nearly $4 billion in protecting the Great Lakes freshwater ecosystem in the last decade, while Canada has invested far less in similar initiatives over the same period.
Sec. 2. Lake America. (a) The body of water currently known as Lake Ontario is a tremendous asset to the United States and part of our Nation’s heritage. With the deepest parts of the Lake’s waters lying within United States territory, the United States claims most of the Lake’s volume. The Lake has long been an integral asset to American exploration, settlement, commerce, and defense. From the colonial period through the early republic, the Lake served as a critical artery for American trade, commerce, and military logistics, including the establishment in Oswego of a historic fort and the first United States port of call from the St. Lawrence Seaway, shipbuilding and naval operations during the War of 1812 at Sackets Harbor and other New York posts, and the movement of goods, settlers, and later industrial cargoes that linked the interior of the United States to eastern markets and the Atlantic. Maritime commerce on the broader Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway system — of which the Lake is the easternmost and gateway segment — continues to generate substantial economic activity for the United States, supporting hundreds of thousands of American jobs and billions of dollars in annual economic output, cargo value, and related business revenue, with our ports, carriers, and States deriving a significant share of the system’s benefits in iron ore, limestone, coal, agricultural products, and other bulk commodities. Water from the Lake is used to supply nuclear, natural gas, and oil-fired power plants and to supply municipal drinking water to nearby communities. United States domestic and cross-border shipping activity on the Great Lakes system has historically underpinned regional manufacturing, steel production, agriculture, and energy supply chains in several States, reflecting the strategic and economic importance of these waters to the United States that continues to this day. The Lake will continue to play a pivotal role in shaping America’s future and the global economy. In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation’s economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America.
(b) Within 30 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of the Interior (Secretary) shall, in coordination with the Board on Geographic Names and consistent with 43 U.S.C. 364 through 364f, take all appropriate actions to rename as “Lake America” the body of water currently named as Lake Ontario, bounded on the south and east by the State of New York, and on the north, west, and southwest by the Canadian province of Ontario. The Secretary, conjointly with the Board on Geographic Names, shall subsequently update the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) to reflect the renaming of the Lake and remove all references to Lake Ontario from the GNIS, consistent with applicable law. The Board on Geographic Names shall provide guidance to ensure all Federal Government references to Lake Ontario, including on executive department and agency maps, contracts, and other documents and communications, shall reflect its renaming.
Sec. 3. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this order shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect:
(i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or the head thereof; or
(ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
(b) This order shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations.
(c) This order is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any other person.
(d) The costs for publication of this order shall be borne by the Department of the Interior.
DONALD J. TRUMP, THE WHITE HOUSE, August 27, 2026.

The Associated Press published this story and InDepthNH.org is republishing it in collaboration with the AP Journalism Fund
By The Associated Press
President Donald Trump said Thursday he is renaming Lake Ontario to be known as “Lake America” in the U.S. as he exacerbates his trade war with Canada. The Republican president signed an executive order updating the lake’s name for the U.S. geographic naming service. Trump cannot, however, force Canada to follow his preferred naming convention.
The president has been floating the idea of the name change in recent days as the U.S. announced it was imposing 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down. Canada struck back on Tuesday, slapping retaliatory tariffs on about $20 billion worth of U.S. goods, from industrial products to everyday purchases.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” invoking the lake’s Indigenous roots while pointedly casting the episode as part of a transformation of the United States under Trump.
In a social media post, Carney noted that Lake Ontario takes its name from the Wendat word “Ontari’io,” meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,” and said the name predates both the Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence.
“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” Carney said.
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”
Canadian historian Robert Bothwell says Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” should be met with ridicule.
“People should be standing around the capital laughing themselves sick,” Bothwell said. “Everybody knows the Gulf of America is a joke, and this is a joke in an awful way.”
Bothwell says the renaming fits what he sees as Trump’s broader effort to subordinate Canada and said it makes a negotiated settlement between the two countries “next to impossible.”
He also warned that if Apple or Google adopt “Lake America” on their maps, it could provoke a backlash in Canada.
“It’s an insult,” Bothwell said, adding that Canadians could respond with boycotts that might grow into a broader political movement.
Canada is bolstering its defense industry as US relations fray.
The Canadian government is investing an additional $60 billion over the next five years to reduce its dependence on American suppliers, a shift due to Trump’s pressure to contribute more to NATO as well as strained trade relations with Washington.
Canada aims to boost domestic defense capabilities and create jobs while developing innovative technologies for military and civilian use, like drones and robotics. Clothing maker Wuxly, known for luxury parkas, is joining in, making high-tech military gear.
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s vow to strengthen Canadian economic self-sufficiency is a boon for Canadian startups and established companies, as well as firms in Europe.

U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.
“We are going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario, effective immediately, to Lake America,” Trump said from the Oval Office Thursday.
Trump’s action comes amidst a trade war with Canada with both countries imposing tariffs on each other's imports.
Last year, Trump changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America.
The new order instructs Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum and the Board on Geographic Names to take action on the Lake Ontario name change within 30 days.
The move will change the name on federal documents, maps and websites. Lake Ontario is one of the Great Lakes.
The move comes after the U.S. and Canada traded new tariffs after the latest trade talks fizzled.
Trump has taunted Canada since his return to the White House last year. That includes talking about Canada becoming the 51st state.
The U.S. is Canada's largest export market, accounting for 72% of Canada's total exports, according to the Pangea Logistics Network.
Canada is the second largest export market for American goods, accounting for 12.6% of total U.S. trade outlays, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.
Some international groups and organizations have not gone along with Trump’s renaming of the Gulf of Mexico.
An indigenous tribe in Canada which counts Lake Ontario among its lands is also no fan of Trump’s renaming order.
"Lake Ontario has existed for thousands of years, long before Canada and the United States became the countries we know today," Mississauga's of the Credit First Nation Chief Margaret Sault told Yahoo News Canada before Trump’s Thursday order.
"You can change a label on a map, but you cannot change the relationship that our people have with these lands and waters," she said. "You cannot rename away our history."
The name Ontario has indigenous roots with meanings such as “great lake,” “beautiful water,” and “sparkling water.”

sources.news_title: Trump Changes Name of Lake Ontario to Lake America
sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday, renaming Lake Ontario Lake America amid trade tensions with Canada.
The move comes less than a week after prospects of a trade deal with Canada collapsed and days after he announced a 50 percent tariff on Canadian autos and steel set to kick in next year.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America. That’s going to take place right now as I sign the order,” Trump said.
The order specifically instructs Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum to update the lake’s name in the Geographic Names Information Service. On Tuesday, the White House shared a video where Trump crossed out Lake Ontario on a map and replaced it with Lake America.
When asked what message the name change sends, Trump said there was “no message” he was sending to Canada, but proceeded to say America’s neighbor to the north has long been “ripping” the United States off.
“As you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly. Even the military, you know, we defend Canada for nothing. We don’t get anything. They don’t pay us to defend Canada, but we defend Canada, and they understand that,” Trump said.
“As an example, we bought icebreakers. They’d like to use them. We have 11 brand new icebreakers coming in. They’d like to use the icebreakers. They don’t pay for anything, and they want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state. But they want to be treated like they’re a state, and so we just can’t do that anymore,” he added.
Trump said that over the past 15 years, the U.S. has been losing an average of $6o billion a year to Canada.
“We lose on average over the last 15 years, $60 billion a year carrying Canada, so we just can’t do it anymore. We love the people of Canada. I don’t think their representatives do an appropriate job. Maybe they’ll change. I really don’t know. It doesn’t make much difference,” he said.
Trump said he has been thinking about the name change for a long time.
“So, the lake change, the Lake of America, was something I’ve been thinking about for a long time. Actually, as you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it, and now it’s very routinely the Gulf of America,” he said
“If you think about it, we have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both,” he added.

President Donald Trump on Thursday followed through on a threat to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” issuing an executive order to “Make the Great Lakes Even Greater” amid a collapsed trade deal with Canada, further escalating tensions between the two former allies.
The lake in question has been known as Lake Ontario since the 1600s. Trump contends that it should be renamed because America spends more money on it than Canada does.

My colleague Alex Nguyen covered Canada’s response to the escalating trade war—a large support package for Canadian workers and firms—on Tuesday:
While the plan aims more at support for businesses than direct funds for individual Canadians, it is a meaningful step that far exceeds any the Trump administration has taken or tried to take, with the White House largely ignoring the foreseeable harm of its tariffs on American workers and consumers… Nearly every state has experienced blue-collar job losses as a result of the tariff agenda, even as the policies deliver few apparent results in improving US manufacturing or lowering the trade deficit.

Trump Officially Rebrands Lake Ontario as 'Lake America' After Trade Talks Explode With Canada
sources.text:
Trump Officially Rebrands Lake Ontario as 'Lake America' After Trade Talks Explode With Canada
Executive order sparks controversy as US-Canada trade talks collapse
Donald Trump has signed an executive order attempting to strike Lake Ontario from the map and replace it with 'Lake America', the latest escalation in a trade war with Canada that has turned personal, petty and increasingly expensive for both countries.
The order, signed in the Oval Office on Thursday 27 August 2026, directs the US Department of the Interior to update federal naming records so that Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes straddling the US-Canadian border, is officially referred to by American agencies as 'Lake America'.
The order instructs the Secretary of the Interior, working with the Board on Geographic Names, to rename the lake bounded on the south and east by New York State and on the north, west and south-west by the Canadian province of Ontario.
It marks Trump's second attempt in 18 months to unilaterally redraw the map in America's favour, following his renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the 'Gulf of America' in January 2025.
What the Executive Order Does and Cannot Do
Signing the order at the Resolute Desk, with a large map showing 'Lake America' stamped over Lake Ontario propped up behind him, Trump told reporters the change was effective 'immediately'. 'We're going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario, effective immediately to Lake America,' he said.
Trump justified the move by pointing to geography, arguing the lake 'has most of its volume in the United States' and that its deepest sections sit in American territory.
The order cites a prior directive, Executive Order 14172, 'Restoring Names That Honour American Greatness', and states it is administration policy to name 'great natural landmarks for our shared achievements'.
Practically, the order's reach is limited. It compels the Interior Department's Geographic Names Information System to reflect the change for federal use, but the president cannot force Canada, international bodies or private companies to adopt the new name.
Responsibility for enacting the switch falls to the US Board on Geographic Names, a body created in 1890 to standardise place names for federal agencies, which follows a formal submission and review process.
A Trade War Turned Personal
The lake row followed the collapse of US-Canada trade talks days earlier, when negotiators failed to finalise a deal ahead of a midnight deadline.
Trade negotiations between the United States and Canada fell apart on Friday night, shortly before a midnight deadline for 50 per cent tariffs to take effect on roughly £14.8bn ($20bn) worth of Canadian products, including dairy goods, alcoholic beverages, cement and hockey equipment.
US Customs and Border Protection issued a bulletin to businesses warning that officers would enforce the new rates immediately once the deadline passed.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney did not hold back. 'You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,' he told reporters, adding that retaliatory tariffs targeting American steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics would take effect on 8 September.
Carney was blunter about the failed talks, saying the United States had 'proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits for Canada', adding: 'In short, they asked too much, and they offered too little.'
Trump's response, posted to Truth Social, was combative: 'Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!! No more!!!' It was against that backdrop, two days before the executive order was signed, that Trump first floated the lake rename as a threat rather than policy.
'The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don't expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer,' he wrote, following it with a doctored map showing 'Lake Ontario' crossed out in favour of gold lettering reading 'Lake America'.
Canada's Strategy Ignore the Taunt and Enforce the Tariff
Canadian officials have largely refused to dignify the taunt. Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's trade minister for relations with the US, declined to address Trump's post, telling CNBC: 'We've decided as a federal government months ago not to respond to sort of the daily social media posts of either the president or his Cabinet secretaries.'
Ontario Premier Doug Ford was more direct, insisting the province and its residents would continue calling the lake by its original name regardless of what Washington's paperwork said.
Asked what message the order sent to Canada, Trump said 'no message', adding Canada had been 'ripping us off for a long time on trade' and America had long defended its northern neighbour 'for nothing'.
The lake's name derives from the Iroquois word for 'great lake', predating the province of Ontario by centuries. Canada had not issued a formal response at time of writing. With retaliatory tariffs due within days and no fresh talks scheduled, the renamed lake may prove the least consequential front in a rapidly widening economic dispute.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump has signed an executive order directing U.S. federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America” in official documents and records.
The move comes amid continuing tensions between Washington and Ottawa over trade. It follows Trump's earlier effort to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America,” continuing his push to alter geographic names through federal action.
Lake Ontario is shared by the United States and Canada, making the directive largely symbolic outside the U.S. government. Canadian authorities have not been required to change their official terminology.
The decision adds another point of friction to already strained U.S.-Canada relations and reflects Trump's broader use of geographic renaming as a political tool.

sources.news_title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America
sources.text:
Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.
The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter tariffs next month.
Trump has repeatedly posted threats about renaming the lake, one of the five Great Lakes that straddle both countries, on social media amid the trade dispute.
He said on Thursday the move was "official, effective immediately" and that his administration has "filed all the necessary papers, documents" to make the change.
Text of the executive order says it gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted the name Lake Ontario can be traced back more than 400 years, adding in a social media post on Thursday that preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.
"We know that the United States is changing. Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms," he wrote. "Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario – today and forever."
When Trump took the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.
It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application.
In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".
The White House at the time also blocked Associated Press reporters from presidential events over the news agency's refusal to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in its coverage. The AP sued the Trump administration in response, and that legal battle is ongoing.
There is no universally recognised international body setting the names of international waters. While the US president has broad discretion over how his country officially recognises landmarks, other countries do not have to follow.
Canada does not have to recognise name changes made by other countries and officials there have dismissed the idea.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote on social media, "It's Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever."
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston agreed, saying "We're into some real foolishness now. It's Lake Ontario, buddy."
"We'll always call it Lake Ontario," said Industry Minister Melanie Joly on Tuesday.
The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York.
As he signed the order on Thursday in the Oval Office, Trump said it wasn't a direct message to Canada, but that America's northern neighbour "has been ripping us off for a long time on trade".
Trump said he'd been thinking about renaming the lake "for a long time".
"So if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake," Trump said.
"Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both."
The name change request comes amid a trade dispute that has seen US-Canada relations fall to new lows, with insults thrown back-and-forth between the Trump administration and Canadian officials over the past week.
There was a hint on Thursday that there was room for a return to the negotiating table sometime in the future.
Canadian US trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, said in a post on X that the US had withdrawn some of its demands around labelling requirements in French "and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future US trade actions".
"We look forward to further constructive US clarifications on their other positions, which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty".
Trade talks collapsed at the last minute late on Friday night, with both sides accusing the other of demanding last-minute changes to a tentative deal.
Democratic lawmaker Debbie Dingell of Michigan, the US state that borders four of the five Great Lakes, said that she would introduce a bill in Congress to nullify the name change, calling Trump's order "idiotic".
She wrote, "The Great Lakes are a shared treasure that generations of Americans and Canadians have worked together to protect".
Other Democratic lawmakers in the US also criticised the order on social media, calling for the Trump administration to get back to negotiating on a trade deal. Some mocked Trump's idea and posted their own ideas to change the names of other landmarks.
Wisconsin's governor joked, "I just renamed Lake Michigan Lake Wisconsin," in a social media post with a video of himself signing a napkin on one of the Great Lakes. "See, I can sign napkins that say things, too," he added.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said her state, the sole US state bordering Lake Ontario, "won't be calling it" Lake America.
Meanwhile, Trump's Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum applauded the move, writing, "We're on it, Mr. President!"
"The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States," he said, adding that the US Geological Survey "maps our country for the world to see, and we are PROUD to implement your Executive Order to rename LAKE AMERICA".

US President Donald Trump has renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America”, escalating a feud with Canada that has already spawned tariffs on tens of billions of dollars in cross-border trade.
The change would take effect immediately, said Trump, who also ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed as the Gulf of America after assuming office last year.

Trump signed an executive order that updated the lake’s name for the US geographic naming service.
The president cannot force Canada to follow his preferred naming convention, however.
Trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed last week with each side blaming the other for derailing three days of intensive negotiations.
One of the five Great Lakes of North America, Lake Ontario borders both the Canadian province of Ontario and the US. state of New York.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the name change in a social media post.
He said Lake Ontario takes its name from the Wendat word “Ontari’io,” meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big” and said the name predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.
“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” Carney said.
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario - then, now and always.”
After Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed in January 2025, it took about two weeks for the US Board on Geographic Names, as part of the Department of the Interior, to update the official federal nomenclature in the Geographic Names Information System to reflect the changes, effective immediately for federal use.
About 52 per cent of the surface area of Lake Ontario is in Canada, with the remainder in New York under a 1909 treaty.

sources.news_title: Trump just renamed Lake Ontario to "Lake America"—and Canada is not happy
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday updating Lake Ontario’s name to “Lake America” for the U.S. geographic naming service amid an ongoing trade war with Canada.
In an X post at 1:26 p.m. on Thursday, the White House shared a map of the Great Lakes with Lake Ontario changed to “Lake America.”
The White House declared that the change is “effective immediately.”
   
       
   
U.S. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum vowed to move forward with the update.
        “We’re on it, Mr. President! The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States,” he stated. “@USGS maps our country for the world to see, and we are PROUD to implement your Executive Order to rename LAKE AMERICA.”
Earlier in the day, Trump proclaimed, “all it takes is a good pen and some intelligence” to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”
        
      The president posted an earlier video of himself on Instagram crossing out Lake Ontario on a map and replacing it with “Lake America” in black marker.
Mark Carney responds
Prime Minister Mark Carney posted a response on X, noting Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”
“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” Carney added.
Carney also referenced the trade war between the U.S. and Canada, accented by new U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods and Canadian counter-tariffs on U.S. products that are slated to take effect Sept. 8.
        “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Vermont Governor Phil Scott called the president’s executive order “petty and disappointing.”
“We should be at the negotiating table, finding a path forward that strengthens both the U.S. and Canadian economies,” he posted to X. “Further escalating tensions does nothing to help American or Canadian families and businesses.”
Trump posts video on World Lake Day
The president’s latest move to rename Lake Ontario comes on the same day as the global community recognizes World Lake Day, a day set aside by the United Nations to recognize fresh water resources and their importance to agriculture and industry.
How did we get here?
On Tuesday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that the U.S. is considering the name change “in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer.”
Later on Tuesday, the president posted an image of a map with Lake Ontario crossed out and replaced with “Lake America.”
Trump took the message a step further.
In a video posted on Truth Social on Thursday, the president declares, “So this is Lake Ontario, in Canada and in the United States. But we’re going to make a little change. We’re going to call it something different than Lake Ontario. We’re going to call it Lake America. And all it takes is a good pen and some intelligence.”
Trump also recalled his efforts to rename the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America, which is now reflected on some maps and mobile apps.
“So now we have a lake and now we have a gulf,” Trump boasted in the video. “Because we have the Gulf of America and we now we have Lake America.”
        ‘How about Lake Epstein?’
While some commenters are supporting the president, including one who proclaimed “Lake America Great Again,” others are trolling the president, including one person who remarked, “How about Lake Epstein?”
How Trump can rename Lake Ontario
In the U.S., the U.S. Board on Geographic Names is the federal body that standardizes names for federal use. The organization, created in 1890, and established in its present form by public law in 1947, maintains uniform geographic name usage throughout the federal government.
For shared bodies of water such as the Great Lakes, naming conventions are embedded in cross-border treaties, federal laws and joint organizations, including the International Joint Commission.
In Canada, the Geographical Names Board of Canada works with provincial and territorial boards to regulate place names.
While Trump can sign executive orders to change the naming practices of the U.S. Board on Geographic Names, Canada is not compelled to accept the new name, and the change could raise a standardization problem between Canada and the U.S.
A United Nations conference report from 1972 states that when countries sharing a given geographical feature and having different official languages do not succeed in agreeing on a common name form, it should be a general rule of international cartography that the name forms of each of the languages in question should be accepted.
“A policy of accepting only one or some of such name forms while excluding the rest on principle would be inconsistent as well as inexpedient in practice. Only technical reasons may sometimes make it necessary, especially in the case of small-scale maps, to dispense with the use of certain name forms belonging to one language or another.”
The document makes no mention of one jurisdiction renaming a shared geographical feature as a measure of economic belligerence, however.
Doug Ford responds to Lake Ontario renaming
        Premier Doug Ford also chimed in, posting to X: “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.”
In an interview with Bloomberg TV on Tuesday, Ford suggested Trump could rename the lake if he wants to, but Ontario would not accept the change.
“I know Canadians. We’re always going to call it Lake Ontario,” Ford said.
Ford also dismissed Trump’s earlier assertion that the U.S. won’t be doing much business with Ontario amid a broader trade war, noting millions of Americans depend on cross-border trade for their incomes.
“He’s saying he won’t do a lot of business with Ontario. Well, let me remind the president: nine million Americans wake up every single morning to produce a product, a widget or a service for Ontario.”
Why some maps show the Gulf of Mexico as the ‘Gulf of America’
As mentioned earlier, Lake Ontario isn’t the first international body of water Trump has moved to rename.
Last year, the U.S. House of Representatives narrowly voted to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” and the change was reflected on some versions of Google Maps.
In a blog post, Google noted the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) was officially updated from “Gulf of Mexico” to “Gulf of America.”
Google said the change was consistent with its “practice of applying name changes when they have been updated in official government sources.”
Today, the semienclosed sea bordered by the United States, Mexico and Cuba is referenced differently on Google Maps, depending upon location.
People using the Google Maps app in the U.S. see “Gulf of America,” while users in Mexico see “Gulf of Mexico.”
App users in the rest of the world, including Canada, see the body of water labelled as “Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America).”

Ford told The Associated Press earlier this week that Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” and “disgusted with President Trump” over Trump’s tariff policies and his departure from Reagan’s free-trade legacy. Trump, in turn, dismissed Ford’s comments as “bluster,” called him Carney’s “flunky” and mocked him as the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother” of the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford.
