The president posted on his social media site depicting himself over images of American flags, an aircraft carrier and jets, as well as a frowning Bush next to a sign reading “Mission Not Accomplished: 2001-2021.”
The post also shows Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed by strikes in February, next to a sign reading “Mission Accomplished 2026.”
Bush stood on an aircraft carrier under a “Mission Accomplished” banner just six weeks into an Iraq war that dragged on for years, a move that came to be seen as a political blunder.
Trump’s latest post also ignores that Trump himself was president for the four years of his first term during the time his post implies U.S. military failure.

Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin and Middle East reporter Lara Korte are named as plaintiffs in the federal lawsuit filed Thursday in Washington, D.C.
The Pentagon, which partially funds the news outlet, fired them last week. A Pentagon spokesperson declined to comment on the lawsuit’s allegations.
Slavin says he was dismissed for insubordination after giving an interview in which he objected to potential censorship by the U.S. military. Korte participated in the same interview. Lederer was dismissed shortly after announcing his impending retirement.
Carney rejects Trump’s ‘Lake America’ renaming with a swipe at a changing US
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” invoking the lake’s Indigenous roots while pointedly casting the episode as part of a transformation of the United States under Trump.
In a social media post, Carney noted that Lake Ontario takes its name from the Wendat word “Ontari’io,” meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,” and said the name predates both the Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence.
“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” Carney said.
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”
Judge questions why Kennedy Center is moving so quickly to return Trump’s name to building
Just seconds after the Trump administration’s lawyer, Bradley Mayers, began making his case at a nearly two-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper interrupted to ask why the Kennedy Center needed to begin inscribing the president’s name on the institution’s facade as soon as Sept. 8.
“What’s magic about that date?” Cooper asked, quipping that sometimes judges travel over the Labor Day holiday.
Mayers responded that the timeline was in accordance with a vote earlier this month by the Trump-aligned board. As he returned to his arguments that renovations at the Kennedy Center require energy and talent, Cooper interjected again.
“That’s all fine and good,” the judge said. “What does that have to do with what Congress intended in these statutes? That’s really what’s before me.”
Canadian histo
rian says ‘Lake America’ move should be mocked, warns of backlash
Canadian historian Robert Bothwell says Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” should be met with ridicule.
“People should be standing around the capital laughing themselves sick,” Bothwell said. “Everybody knows the Gulf of America is a joke, and this is a joke in an awful way.”
Bothwell says the renaming fits what he sees as Trump’s broader effort to subordinate Canada and said it makes a negotiated settlement between the two countries “next to impossible.
He also warned that if Apple or Google adopt “Lake America” on their maps, it could provoke a backlash in Canada.
“It’s an insult,” Bothwell said, adding that Canadians could respond with boycotts that might grow into a broader political movement.
DOJ sues 4 more states for offering in-state tuition for immigrant students
The U.S. Department of Justice is suing four states that provide in-state tuition for students without legal status, saying the practice discriminates against U.S. citizens and encourages illegal immigration.
The complaints against Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon and Washington were filed Thursday, marking just the latest legal challenges over tuition breaks for such students. In all, the department has filed 21 lawsuits, with five of those resulting in judges permanently enjoining and declaring unconstitutional laws that gave reduced tuition to students living in the U.S. illegally.
“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said in a statement. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”
Federal prosecutors are seeking to keep the four states from providing in-state tuition rates for all immigrants who maintain in-state residency, regardless of whether those students are lawfully present in the United States.
New analysis says the Trump administration’s logic used to cut emissions rules is flawed
The Trump administration relied on flawed logic to justify scrapping vehicle emissions standards earlier this year, according to a new study by a group of economists published Thursday in the journal Science.
It scrapped the emissions standards when it revoked the endangerment finding, which had long served as the legal underpinning for federal regulation of greenhouse gas emissions.
Researchers who examined the Environmental Protection Agency’s analysis for doing so said eliminating the rules will cost the country billions of dollars, not save it billions.
Even setting aside environmental reasons for keeping emissions rules, “the economic case for the rollback of the standards still falls apart,” said Antonio Bento, one of the study’s authors.
The EPA said it stands by its economic analysis.
“We will not attempt to push an EV mandate on the American people based on facially implausible projections,” the agency said in a statement.
Democratic-led states sue Trump administration over changes to family planning program
The program provides grants to health care providers for contraception, cancer screenings and other services, mainly for low-income women.
More than 20 states, including New York, Massachusetts and California, argue in a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services that the department broke the law when it set stricter rules this year for which providers qualify for the program, including requiring them to end diversity programs.
“This lawsuit is about ensuring safe and effective family planning and reproductive care remains accessible to all,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said at a news conference, adding that the new requirements were politically motivated.
Democrat who questioned Kennedy about his 2019 Samoa trip says the now-health secretary lied
During Kennedy’s confirmation hearings to be the nation’s health secretary, Sen. Edward Markey, D-Mass., asked about Kennedy’s 2019 trip to Samoa at least three times.
Again and again, Kennedy denied that his reason for the trip was related to vaccines.
Markey said new documents published by the AP and The Guardian on Thursday “confirm what we already knew: RFK Jr. lied to Congress.”
“This is a pattern, not a slip,” Markey said in a statement. “He should never have been confirmed, and he cannot be trusted to run HHS for even one more day.”
In response to questions from the AP, the Department of Health and Human Services said that the Samoa visit “was unrelated to vaccines.”
But the US president can’t dictate what the rest of the world calls it
Trump has wide latitude over how the U.S. government recognizes geographic places and landmarks.
But he can’t force Canada or individual citizens on either side of the border to follow his preferred naming conventions.
Trump introduced idea to rename Lake Ontario hours before Canada announced its reciprocal tariffs
“The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer,” Trump posted Tuesday on Truth Social.
This latest branding move — reminiscent of his move to rechristen the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” — highlights how much Trump’s rhetoric and trade policy have sundered the previously warm relationship between Washington and Ottawa.
In a scheduled announcement hours after Trump’s post, Canadian leaders unveiled tariffs on about $20 billion worth of American goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment — a retaliation for the Trump administration’s new 50% tariffs on Canadian goods.
Lake Ontario’s name predates either country
The lake’s name comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” meaning “lake of shining waters,” and predates European settlement in the region. The province, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
The International Hydrographic Organization — of which both the United States and Canada are members — works to ensure that the world’s seas, oceans and navigable waters are surveyed and charted uniformly, and also names some of them. But there is no single international body that determines the names of international bodies of water.
Lutnick downplays potential of demolishing Kennedy Center
Trump administration lawyers raised the prospect earlier this week that the Kennedy Center would be demolished if Trump’s name wasn’t recognized at the institution to facilitate further fundraising for renovations.
“What was pointed out,” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told reporters, “was that if you do nothing, bad things happen. But they’re not going to happen on Thursday.”
Lutnick was speaking ahead of a hearing in Washington to consider arguments over the Kennedy Center’s move to inscribe Trump’s name on the building. He argued that the effort was a way to recognize the president’s contributions to the renovations and said the board wasn’t trying to rename the institution, which a judge ruled earlier this year was illegal.
“That’s yesterday,” Lutnick said of the renaming debate.
Trump sidesteps question about CIA director’s Russia trip
CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise visit to Moscow earlier this week, but Trump won’t share what he told Russian officials.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing unidentified people briefed on the matter, that Ratcliffe’s trip was to deliver a warning to Russia not to attack NATO countries.
Asked during Thursday’s Oval Office exchange with reporters about whether Ratcliffe delivered that message to Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump offered a roundabout response.
“I don’t want to comment on that, but they’re not going to attack,” Trump said.
Trump says US is sending aid to Nepal after catastrophic floods
The president said recent flooding in a border area of China and Nepal was terrible to see, describing how “strong, well-built buildings were wiped out like they were toothpicks.”
Talking to reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday, he said the U.S. has spoken with Nepalese leaders and offered to provide “anything they want.”
Trump said there were 50 or 60 Americans in the area but added that a full accounting hasn’t been completed.
The State Department has said 90 Americans were unaccounted for in China and Nepal. It said it was not aware of any U.S. deaths.
Hawaii governor condemns RFK Jr.’s 2019 Samoa trip and says health secretary ‘misled Congress’
Hawaii’s Democratic Gov. Josh Green on Thursday called for Kennedy to resign as health secretary, saying he “misled Congress about his intentions in Samoa and his stance on vaccinations during his confirmation hearings.”
The statement came in reaction to new reporting from the AP and The Guardian revealing that documents refute Kennedy’s statements to senators that a 2019 trip he took to Samoa had “nothing to do with vaccines.”
Green, a Democrat and physician, organized flights loaded with vaccine doses to administer inoculations in Samoa during its deadly measles outbreak later in 2019.
Green said Kennedy’s “fear tactics” contributed to that disaster.
“He and his anti-vax organization intentionally misled the Prime Minister and the people of Samoa about the measles vaccination earlier that year, and Samoa paid the ultimate price,” Green said.
Trump calls Cruz ‘very talented,’ says the Texas senator ‘might’ run for president in 2028
The president was asked about Cruz teasing a 2028 presidential run and responded, “I would say that he’s very talented. He’s a very good friend of mine. I think he might do that, yeah.”
Trump added of Cruz: “He’s a talented guy.”
Cruz ran for president in 2016 and was among the last Republican primary candidates still in the race when Trump clinched the party’s nomination.
Trump signs order renaming Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ in the US
Trump said Thursday he is renaming Lake Ontario to be known as “Lake America” in the United States as he exacerbates his trade war with Canada.
The Republican president signed an executive order that updated the lake’s name for the U.S. geographic naming service. Trump cannot force Canada to follow his preferred naming convention, however. The move is reminiscent of his move last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.’”
Trump, who signed the order as he was sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, had a large sign behind him propped on a stand with a map of the Great Lakes. Over Lake Ontario, in big red letters, the map read “Lake America.”
He told reporters that Canada is “the worst” to deal with on trade. “They feel entitled and we can’t have that,” he said.
The president has been floating the idea of the name change in recent days as the U.S. announced it was imposing 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down.
Democratic senator who questioned Kennedy on Samoa reacts to AP’s reporting
AP’s latest findings about Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ’s trip to Samoa show his platform “is built on lies and grifts that leave a trail of dead children in their wake,” said Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, which oversees Kennedy’s health department.
The AP reported earlier Thursday that new documents refute Kennedy’s account that his 2019 visit, before a deadly measles outbreak, had “nothing to do with vaccines.”
Responding to the reporting, Wyden said he plans to press Republicans to refer Kennedy to the Justice Department for criminal investigation for lying to Congress.
If Democrats take the Senate majority in this fall’s elections, he added, his committee will prioritize holding Kennedy accountable.
“There are consequences for lying to Congress,” he said.
Group of Democratic senators calls on ICE to cancel plan for shock gloves
A group of U.S. senators led by Democrat Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada is urging Immigration and Customs Enforcement to cancel its plan to outfit officers with gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks.
In a letter to ICE’s acting director, Cortez Masto and 15 of her colleagues in the Democratic caucus questioned ICE’s need to spend up to $20 million on the devices and the agency’s ability to use them appropriately.
“The blatant and tragic misuse of force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, Houston, Maine, and other locations around the country raises significant skepticism about the agency’s professional capability to safely deploy a new tool that could be used to harm Americans without cause,” the letter said.
Zelenskyy’s direct plea helped unlock Russia sanctions in the Senate. What’s next is uncertain
A Russian sanctions package in Congress represents the most ambitious effort to support Ukraine since Trump returned to the White House. The Senate approved it after a personal plea from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who told lawmakers after Lindsey Graham’s funeral last month that his country needs the sanctions as a morale booster.
The bill Graham promoted would deprive President Vladimir Putin of oil and gas revenue fueling the war machine. But House approval is uncertain. House Speaker Mike Johnson faces resistance from some Republicans. And many Democrats supportive of Ukraine warn it would hand Trump too much tariff authority.
The shortage illustrates cascading fallout from Trump’s unexpected war against Iran
U.S. missile stocks in Europe have been moved to the Middle East, where U.S. and Gulf allies have fired off significant numbers of interceptors, including Patriots, to thwart Iran’s drones and missiles. Some of those attacks have killed and wounded American troops.
Though a Russian ballistic missile attack against NATO countries is not imminently expected, CIA Director John Ratcliffe went to Moscow this week to warn Russia not to attack, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump played down the significance of the rare and secretive trip, saying it was “sort of semi-routine.”
European and NATO officials say Russia could be in a position to attack countries in the alliance by 2030. Patriot stockpiles are projected to rebound by then. In the meantime, Russia’s war in Ukraine could hinder its ability to carry out any missile attack on Europe as it would be a challenge for Moscow to fight an air war on two fronts.
US faces critical shortage of Patriot missiles in Europe, officials tell AP
The shortage of advanced missile interceptors is largely driven by Trump’s war with Iran, a U.S. defense official in Europe and a NATO official told The Associated Press, raising concerns about vulnerabilities in NATO countries to a potential Russian attack.
The U.S. defense official said the most concerning shortfall involves Patriot missile interceptors, which can shoot down Russia’s high-speed ballistic missiles. The NATO official confirmed the low inventories of Patriots among American and NATO forces in Europe. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.
In the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault on, for example, a military headquarters or power plant, NATO could be in a similar position to Patriot-starved Ukraine and be forced “to take punch after punch in the mouth,” the U.S. defense official said.
In Europe, the American military “definitely” does not have enough Patriots to stop any possible sustained ballistic missile attack and would have “very limited” capability to defend against a single ballistic missile strike or a stray Russian missile that goes off course, the U.S. official said.
Michigan Democrats want to fight Trump. First they have to stop fighting each other
When Democrats gathered this week in a West Michigan congressional district they’re trying to flip blue, they wanted to talk about the cost of living under President Donald Trump. But it didn’t take long for the conversation to turn to a controversy dividing their party.
One attendee chided U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten for failing to support Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
“Your inflammatory rhetoric has nothing to do with creating a better economic future for the people of West Michigan, and everything to do with protecting the pipeline of our tax dollars to Israel,” the woman said.
The exchange captured a problem confronting Democrats as they head toward November. Party leaders believe concerns about the economy have given them an opening to win control of Congress, but internal divisions are making it harder to keep the focus there.
New sanctions and a trade embargo leave Iran with few places to turn
Iran’s economy, already strained by high inflation, years of Western sanctions and a war that has sharply reduced oil revenue, is poised for more instability as the Trump administration tries to coerce other countries into ending all financial dealings with the Islamic Republic.
A decision by the United Arab Emirates to suspend trade relations with Iran last week kick-started the White House’s latest attempt to isolate Tehran into submission. Iran entered the war with its foreign commerce concentrated among a relatively small group of countries, leaving it with fewer places to turn now.
The success of the U.S. strategy will largely hinge on China, the main buyer of Iranian oil and its top trading partner. Russia, a fellow target of sweeping U.S.-led sanctions, has a military conflict and economic crisis of its own and probably can’t offer longtime ally Iran much hard financial support.
Canada is bolstering its defense industry as US relations fray
The Canadian government is investing an additional $60 billion over the next five years to reduce its dependence on American suppliers, a shift due to Trump’s pressure to contribute more to NATO as well as strained trade relations with Washington.
Canada aims to boost domestic defense capabilities and create jobs while developing innovative technologies for military and civilian use, like drones and robotics. Clothing maker Wuxly, known for luxury parkas, is joining in, making high-tech military gear.
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s vow to strengthen Canadian economic self-sufficiency is a boon for Canadian startups and established companies, as well as firms in Europe.

sources.text:
Trump orders Lake Ontario to be renamed ‘Lake America’ amid Canada trade war
Updated ,first published
Washington: Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario – which sits between the US and Canada – to “Lake America” amid an ongoing trade war between the two North American neighbours and allies.
The US president’s order instructs his interior secretary, Doug Burgum, to change the lake’s official name in the US through the Geographic Names Information System, and remove all references to Lake Ontario on department and agency maps, contracts and other documents.
Trump made the announcement in the Oval Office with an enlarged map of Lake Ontario with the words “Lake America” stamped over it in red, as well as a cardboard sign that said: “Making the Great Lakes Even Greater”.
He floated the change several days ago after a trade war with Canada escalated on the weekend. Prime Minister Mark Carney withdrew from trade negotiations saying the Americans had made a series of last-minute changes and demands that were unacceptable to Canada.
Canada will now impose 50 per cent tariffs on about $US20 billion ($28 billion) worth of additional American goods, matching the 50 per cent US tariffs that began on Saturday.
“Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly,” Trump said on Thursday (Washington time). “They don’t pay us to defend Canada, but we defend Canada. They don’t pay for anything.
“But they want to be treated like they’re a [US] state. We just can’t do that any more.” He said his problem was with Canadian government officials, who were “nasty people” and “entitled”, not the people of Canada.
White House staff secretary Ben Moss added: “This is a lake that has most of its volume in the United States. The deepest parts of the lakes are in United States territory. So, this will reflect that this is an American lake.”
The move is reminiscent of Trump’s decision early in his second term to name the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America”, a change that has been partly adopted by other organisations. For example, Google Maps shows the body of water as the Gulf of America.
Trump added that he had been thinking about changing the name of Lake Ontario for a long time. “We have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean,” he said. “So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific [oceans]. Maybe we’ll change them both.”
The International Hydrographic Organisation – of which both the United States and Canada are members – works to ensure that the world’s seas, oceans and navigable waters are surveyed and charted uniformly, and also names some of them. But there is no single international body that determines names of international bodies of water.
The US and Canada share borders along multiple Great Lakes, including Lake Ontario, which sits between Canada’s Ontario province and upstate New York State. Ontario is also the single largest export destination for more than a dozen US states.
Responding to Trump’s announcement, Carney noted the name Lake Ontario came from the word “Ontari’io”, belonging to the native Wendat people of the Great Lakes, which meant “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big”.
The name predates European settlement and, as Carney noted, the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America.
“We know that America is changing,” he wrote on X. “Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Hours after Trump hosted his Oval Office news conference, he posted a note on social media from Ned Mamula, director of the US Geological Survey, affirming that the change had been made.
With AP

sources.news_title: Trump Changes Name of Lake Ontario to Lake America: Read the Full Executive Order
sources.text:
Trump Changes Name of Lake Ontario to Lake America: Read the Full Executive Order
President Donald Trump is renaming yet another body of water.
After the 80-year-old President of the United States renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America last year, he has just signed an executive order on Thursday (August 27) renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” and the change is “effectively immediately” amid trade tensions between the United States and Canada.
Why Is Donald Trump Renaming Lake Ontario?
“As I announced in Executive Order 14172 of January 20, 2025 (Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness), it is the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements,” he declared in the executive order.
“The United States is the greatest protector of the Great Lakes, including the body of water currently known as Lake Ontario. Without the security and investment provided by the United States, this freshwater system would not be open for shipping, recreation, and responsible use to the same extent as it is today. The United States Coast Guard supplies 9 of the 11 ice breaking vessels on the Great Lakes, securing commercial shipping lanes free of charge. The United States has invested nearly $4 billion in protecting the Great Lakes freshwater ecosystem in the last decade, while Canada has invested far less in similar initiatives over the same period.”
Where is Lake Ontario?
Lake Ontario is located in North America, bordered by Ontario to the north and New York to the south. It is the smallest and easternmost of the five Great Lakes.
What Does the Executive Order Say?
Read the full executive order via the White House inside…
By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered:
Section 1. Purpose and Policy. As I announced in Executive Order 14172 of January 20, 2025 (Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness), it is the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements. The United States is the greatest protector of the Great Lakes, including the body of water currently known as Lake Ontario. Without the security and investment provided by the United States, this freshwater system would not be open for shipping, recreation, and responsible use to the same extent as it is today. The United States Coast Guard supplies 9 of the 11 ice breaking vessels on the Great Lakes, securing commercial shipping lanes free of charge. The United States has invested nearly $4 billion in protecting the Great Lakes freshwater ecosystem in the last decade, while Canada has invested far less in similar initiatives over the same period.
Sec. 2. Lake America. (A) The body of water currently known as Lake Ontario is a tremendous asset to the United States and part of our Nation’s heritage. With the deepest parts of the Lake’s waters lying within United States territory, the United States claims most of the Lake’s volume. The Lake has long been an integral asset to American exploration, settlement, commerce, and defense. From the colonial period through the early republic, the Lake served as a critical artery for American trade, commerce, and military logistics, including the establishment in Oswego of a historic fort and the first United States port of call from the St. Lawrence Seaway, shipbuilding and naval operations during the War of 1812 at Sackets Harbor and other New York posts, and the movement of goods, settlers, and later industrial cargoes that linked the interior of the United States to eastern markets and the Atlantic. Maritime commerce on the broader Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway system — of which the Lake is the easternmost and gateway segment — continues to generate substantial economic activity for the United States, supporting hundreds of thousands of American jobs and billions of dollars in annual economic output, cargo value, and related business revenue, with our ports, carriers, and States deriving a significant share of the system’s benefits in iron ore, limestone, coal, agricultural products, and other bulk commodities. Water from the Lake is used to supply nuclear, natural gas, and oil-fired power plants and to supply municipal drinking water to nearby communities. United States domestic and cross-border shipping activity on the Great Lakes system has historically underpinned regional manufacturing, steel production, agriculture, and energy supply chains in several States, reflecting the strategic and economic importance of these waters to the United States that continues to this day. The Lake will continue to play a pivotal role in shaping America’s future and the global economy. In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation’s economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America.
(b) Within 30 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of the Interior (Secretary) shall, in coordination with the Board on Geographic Names and consistent with 43 U.S.C. 364 through 364f, take all appropriate actions to rename as “Lake America” the body of water currently named as Lake Ontario, bounded on the south and east by the State of New York, and on the north, west, and southwest by the Canadian province of Ontario. The Secretary, conjointly with the Board on Geographic Names, shall subsequently update the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) to reflect the renaming of the Lake and remove all references to Lake Ontario from the GNIS, consistent with applicable law. The Board on Geographic Names shall provide guidance to ensure all Federal Government references to Lake Ontario, including on executive department and agency maps, contracts, and other documents and communications, shall reflect its renaming.
Sec. 3. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this order shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect:
(i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or the head thereof; or
(ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
(B) This order shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations.
(C) This order is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any other person.
(D) The costs for publication of this order shall be borne by the Department of the Interior.
DONALD J. TRUMP
THE WHITE HOUSE,
August 27, 2026.

Breaking: Trump Signs 'Lake America' Executive Order 'Effective Immediately'
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America amid a tariff dispute with Canada that has escalated over the past several days.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario, effective immediately, to Lake America,” Trump told reporters inside the Oval Office. “That’s going to take place right now as I sign the order.”
The order will direct Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to update the Geographic Names Information System and certify the change within 30 days.

The United States Coast Guard supplies 9 of the 11 ice breaking vessels on the Great Lakes, securing commercial shipping lanes free of charge.”

Trump’s action comes just days after he targeted Canada on social media, accusing America’s neighbor of profiting from unfair trade deals, before promising punitive tariffs to help even things out.

Trump, who’s known for valuing symbolism, has already changed the name of the Department of Defense to the Department of War, and changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

sources.news_title: President Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America effective immediately.
The executive order directs Secretary Doug Burgum and the Department of the interior to update the Geographic Names Information Service to reflect that the lake, known internationally as Lake Ontario, will be called Lake America in the United States.
The president has significant leeway to change the official names of geographic locations in the United States but lacks authority to dictate the globally accepted names. When the president signed an order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America in 2025, some countries declined to make any change in how they referred to that body of water.
The stated justification from the administration centered on the fact that most of the lake's volume sits in the deepest parts of the lake falling within the geographic area of the United States.
President Trump said the order was already official and that his administration had completed the required paperwork and notifications.
When asked what message the move sent to Canada, the President said it wasn't meant as a message but shifted to trade and military complaints involving Canada.
"No message," Trump said. "As you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade."
President Trump also said Canada had not treated the United States well and pointed to possible tariffs on cars coming from Canada.
"We're going to be doing tariffs on their cars that are coming in at a substantial level," Trump said.
Trump said he had been considering the change for a while.
"Lake America is something I've been thinking about for a long time, actually," Trump said. "As you know, we, took something called the Gulf of Mexico, but we changed it. And now it's very routinely the Gulf of America."

sources.text:
President Donald Trump's fight with Canada has spilled into Lake Ontario — er, Lake America?
On Thursday, Trump signed an executive order that he said would "immediately" rename the body of water to "Lake America." Canadian officials have said they will not recognize the new name.
The order directs the US government to adopt "Lake America" as the official name for federal maps, contracts, and documents. It does not require private map providers to adopt the change. Apple and Google didn't immediately respond to questions about whether they would update their maps.
The move comes as relations between Washington and Ottawa rapidly deteriorate. Trade talks between the neighboring countries broke down on Friday, which prompted new tariffs from the US. Canada responded with its own tariffs, while Trump is threatening potential 50% tariffs on auto and steel imports from Canada, set for January 1.
Trump had threatened to rename the lake several times since the tensions flared.
In a video posted to Truth Social, Trump said renaming the lake only required "a good pen and some intelligence," while crossing out the name on a paper map.
"We're on it, Mr. President," Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote on X. "The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States."
He's already published a secretarial order to the Board on Geographic Names to "immediately rename the body of water known as Lake Ontario to Lake America."
Mark Carney, the Canadian Prime Minister, wrote in a post on X that "naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario."
"The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari'io, which, appropriately, means 'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big'," Carney said.
"The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America," Carney added.
Several Democratic leaders mocked the renaming. Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers posted a video of himself signing a restaurant napkin that declared Lake Michigan "Lake Wisconsin."
"See, I can sign napkins that say things, too," he wrote.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul had a blunter response.
The lake — whichever name you give it — runs along New York State's northwest and Ontario's southwest borders. It's the smallest of the Great Lakes by surface area.
In the executive order, the US said it invested nearly $4 billion in "protecting the Great Lakes freshwater ecosystem in the last decade," including providing nine of the eleven ice-breaking vessels.
According to a US Geological Survey update, the agency is updating the Geographic Names Information System to reflect the change.
It's the second time that Trump has renamed a major body of water during his second term. In January 2025, he signed an executive order to rename the "Gulf of Mexico" the "Gulf of America."
The change could soon extend beyond federal records and appear on widely used digital maps.
GNIS name changes have been cited by Google in the past as a reason to update names on its map. When Mexico threatened legal action against Google over "Gulf of America" map changes following Trump's executive order, the tech company responded in a letter that the change was made to reflect an update from the GNIS and would only be visible to US-based users. Google added in the letter that Google Maps users in Mexico would continue to see "Gulf of Mexico," while people elsewhere in the world would be shown both names.
MapQuest, the go-to directions website before Google Maps dominated the market, made it clear that they will not be changing the lake's name.
The site posted a map of the lake on X, with "Lake Are We Doing This Again?" written over it. The photo was made using MapQuest's "Name Your Own Gulf" feature, a playful webpage that lets users type any name for a location and generates a shareable map displaying that label. The feature was launched after Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico.
We're not changing the name of Lake Ontario. Name it whatever you want at your leisure: https://t.co/E2I0Ezd57W
(tag us so we can see your work 🙂) pic.twitter.com/x8lIAMt6ab
Users quickly posted their own names for the lake using the feature. Some new names created for the lake include "Lake Epstein Files," "Lake of Hormuz," and "Lake Gulf of Mexico."

Lake Ontario is the smallest of the five Great Lakes by surface area. It lies between New York and the Canadian province of Ontario, with the international boundary running through the water. Roughly 53 percent of the lake lies on the Canadian side.

sources.news_title: Trump signs executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday directing the federal government to renam Lake Ontario as Lake America for official U.S. government use, citing American history, commerce and environmental spending on the Great Lakes as trade tensions with Canada intensified.
The order directs the secretary of the interior to work with the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to update federal maps, the Geographic Names Information System and other government documents within 30 days. It applies to the body of water bordered by New York to the south and east and the Canadian province of Ontario to the north, west and southwest.
“The body of water currently known as Lake Ontario is a tremendous asset to the United States and part of our Nation’s heritage,” the order states. It notes that the deepest parts of the lake lie in U.S. territory and that the United States “claims most of the Lake’s volume.” The document traces the lake’s role in colonial-era trade, War of 1812 naval operations at Sackets Harbor, New York, and modern shipping of iron ore, limestone, coal and agricultural products.
Trump signed the order in the Oval Office beside a map labeled “Lake America” and a display titled “Making the Great Lakes Even Greater.”
“The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people,” Trump said. “People oftentimes, they’ll ask me, ‘Who’s the worst to deal with on trade?’ And I say, ‘That’s easy — Canada.’ They feel entitled, and we can’t have that.”
The order describes the United States is “the greatest protector of the Great Lakes.” It says the U.S. Coast Guard provides nine of 11 ice-breaking vessels on the lakes at no charge and that the United States has invested nearly $4 billion in Great Lakes ecosystem protection over the past decade, “while Canada has invested far less in similar initiatives over the same period.” Water from the lake supplies power plants and municipal drinking water, the order adds.
The action follows Trump’s January 2025 order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America and an earlier policy directive to restore names “that honor American greatness.” Trump first floated the Lake Ontario change on Truth Social on Tuesday, writing that the United States did not expect to do “much business with Ontario any longer.”
The renaming applies only to U.S. federal references. Canada and other countries are not required to use the new name, similar to the mixed international recognition of “Gulf of America.”
Trump also addressed an unrelated question during the Oval Office appearance, offering U.S. aid after a tragedy in Nepal.
“It’s terrible. We’ve called Nepal; we’ve offered any help that they need,” he said. “We’re sending aid, and we’ve spoken to the leadership and we let them know anything they want, we’ll have.”
The move comes as the United States and Canada exchange retaliatory tariffs after trade talks collapsed last week. Trump has threatened additional 50% duties on Canadian autos, parts and steel beginning in 2027. Canada announced matching counter-tariffs on about $20 billion in U.S. goods set to take effect Sept. 8. Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Trump have traded personal insults in recent days.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s department is charged with implementing the name change in coordination with the Board on Geographic Names under existing federal statutes governing domestic geographic names. Federal agencies will be instructed to use “Lake America” on maps, contracts and communications.

sources.text:
Trump renames Lake Ontario to Lake America in executive order
Following through on his threat to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America amid a trade battle with Canada, President Donald Trump signed an executive order making the change.
"With the deepest parts of the Lake’s waters lying within United States territory, the United States claims most of the Lake’s volume," reads his order signed Thursday, Aug. 27. "In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation’s economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America."
The move comes after trade negotiations with Canada fell apart, prompting new tariffs.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has escalated tensions with the United States' northern neighbor, referring to Canada as the "51st state." In Michigan, rising tensions and economic strain between the two countries have coincided with a drop in Canadian tourism.
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's communications director Bobby Leddy called the order "a distraction" in a statement. "The fact is our relationship with Canada supports hundreds of thousands of jobs on both sides of the border. The governor's concern right now is the 50% tariff on autos and steel, which will make things more expensive for Michiganders and lead to layoffs," he said.
While Lake Ontario doesn't border Michigan, the move by Trump is likely to become political fodder in the battleground Great Lakes State. Michigan Democrats have railed against the tariffs, arguing they compound cost-of-living challenges under Trump as they run against candidates backed by the president in key races for governor and Congress.
Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson – Michigan Democrats' pick to be the state's next governor – blasted Trump's order. "Canada is our closest ally and our biggest customer. Treating them like an enemy is a gift to China, and Michigan pays for it," she said in a statement. A spokesperson for GOP gubernatorial nominee U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In a post on X, former health official and Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed used Trump's order to mock his Republican opponent, former Congressman Mike Rogers of White Lake, crossing out Lake Michigan to rename it to Lake Florida. Democrats have frequently attacked Rogers' move to Florida after leaving Congress. A spokesperson for Rogers did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Trump's order.
Some have taken to social media to note that the acronym often used to refer to the Great Lakes of Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior – "HOMES" – would spell out "SHAME" with the name change to Lake America.
Like a previous executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, the latest geographic name change ordered by Trump applies to federal maps and documents.

sources.news_title: Trump signs order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America in provocation to Canada
sources.text:
Trump signs order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America in provocation to Canada
Donald Trump signed an order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America for US official use. Lake Ontario is one of North America's five Great Lakes and forms part of the border between Canada's Ontario province and New York state.
US President Donald Trump has signed an order renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America", in a provocative move likely to anger Canada as tensions between the two neighbours remain high over trade. The lake is shared by the United States and Canada, with about 52 per cent of its surface area lying in Canada, making Trump's decision particularly sensitive in Ottawa.
"We're going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday.
"The lake change, the Lake of America, was something I've been thinking about for a long time, actually," he said.
The move adds another layer to an already strained US-Canada relationship, with US tariffs on Canadian goods already fuelling tensions between the two neighbours. Trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed last week after three days of negotiations, with both sides blaming the other for the breakdown.
TRUMP'S LATEST PROVOCATION AGAINST CANADA
Lake Ontario is one of North America's five Great Lakes and forms part of the border between Canada's Ontario province and New York state. While the US President can direct how federal agencies refer to a geographic feature, changing the name in American government records does not automatically mean Canada will recognise the new designation.
The proposed renaming is also notable because Lake Ontario is a shared body of water. Under a 1909 treaty, roughly 52 per cent of its surface area is in Canada, with the rest in New York.
Trump has previously used geographic names as a way of asserting an American identity. After taking office last year, he ordered the Gulf of Mexico to be renamed the "Gulf of America" for US federal use.
US-CANADA TARIFF WAR DEEPENS
The Lake Ontario order comes against the backdrop of Trump's repeated pressure on Canada, including his calls for the country to become the 51st US state, and an escalating tariff war. Washington imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian imports after trade talks collapsed, while Canada has responded with tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on about 700 US products, covering a range of goods in retaliation. The Canadian measures are due to take effect on September 8.
The latest breakdown in trade negotiations has further complicated the relationship, with neither side publicly indicating that a breakthrough is imminent. Trump's approach, however, does not appear to reflect broader American public sentiment towards Canada. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in May found that 72 per cent of Americans had a favourable view of Canada, the highest rating for any country included in the survey.
Trump's Lake Ontario order follows the administration's earlier push to change the Gulf of Mexico's name.
After Trump ordered the change in January 2025, the US Board on Geographic Names, which operates under the Interior Department, updated the federal Geographic Names Information System roughly two weeks later.
That change applied to US federal usage and did not compel other countries or international organisations to adopt the new name.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday, renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” It comes just days after the president said he was considering doing so, amid a trade war with Canada.
“The United States is the greatest protector of the Great Lakes, including the body of water currently known as Lake Ontario. Without the security and investment provided by the United States, this freshwater system would not be open for shipping, recreation, and responsible use to the same extent as it is today,” the executive order says.

The order goes on to say the U.S. has invested more in the lake and Great Lakes freshwater ecosystems over the last decade than Canada has.
Trump shared the news on Truth Social, saying, “Lake Ontario, that’s gone, Lake… America. So now we have… a lake, and now we have… a gulf, because we have the Gulf of America, and now we have Lake America, without the of.”

“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” Carney wrote.
Ongoing trade disputes
Last weekend, Trump ordered new 50% tariffs on Canada after a trade deal between the two countries fell apart.
In response, Canada announced retaliatory tariffs against the U.S. on Tuesday, saying the countermeasures will match U.S. tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.”
Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said the new duties range from 15% to 50% and will take effect on Sept. 8. They focus on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.

sources.news_title: Carney says Lake Ontario will not become 'Lake America'
sources.text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Lake Ontario will continue to be called by that name after US President Donald Trump said he was renaming it as "Lake America."
"The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America," Mr Carney said on X.
"Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario - then, now and always."
Mr Trump signed an order in the White House in a move that comes amid a spiraling trade war between the world's largest economy and its northern neighbour.
"We're going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America," the 80-year-old Republican told reporters in the Oval Office.
"The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They're nasty people."
It comes as Canada's top negotiator in US trade talks sounded a positive note on Washington's position regarding French language and Canadian culture, as Ottawa separately exempted seafood products from planned counter-tariffs.
"The lake change, Lake of America, was something I've been thinking about for a long time, actually. As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it, and now it's very routinely the Gulf of America," Mr Trump said.
"So, if you think about it, we have a Gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both."
Canada did not immediately comment but is unlikely to accept the renaming of Lake Ontario, the smallest of the five Great Lakes by surface area, which borders Canada's Ontario province and New York state.
US-Canada trade talks collapsed at the eleventh hour last week, with Mr Trump's tariffs taking effect on Saturday.
Canada responded with tit-for-tat tariffs on Tuesday, with its Prime Minister saying: "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked."
The same day, Mr Trump announced that he was giving "serious consideration" to changing the name to Lake America.
He then posted a TikTok video late yesterday saying that he intended to do so after all.
The name change - which Canada is unlikely to accept - mirrors Mr Trump's changing of the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in January 2025.
That change obliged the US federal government to refer to the gulf by the new designation, although Mexico has rejected any move to rename it and it lacks international recognition.
While Lake Ontario shares its name with the Canadian province, the name itself is derived from the indigenous Huron word "Ontari'io," which means "great lake" or "beautiful water," according to the National Museum of the Great Lakes.
Toronto, Canada's largest city, sits on its northwestern shore.
During his second presidential term, Mr Trump has irked a series of allies with his outlandish territorial claims, including that Canada should become the 51st US state.
Mr Trump has also laid claim to Greenland, an autonomous territory of NATO ally Denmark, and talked about making Venezuela a state following the US capture of its leader Nicolas Maduro.
In recent days, he has also said that he will make the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman a US territory, despite the fact that the war with Tehran remains ongoing.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America.”
The move comes amid the president’s repeated threats and taunts that he would do so amid his escalating trade war with Canada.
“This is official, effective immediately,” Trump said after signing the order in the Oval Office.

Asked what message he was trying to send Canada by renaming the Great Lake, Trump said, “No message. As you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade.”
“They don’t pay for anything, and they want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state,” Trump said.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted on X a short time after Trump’s action that the name predates Canada — and the U.S.
“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big’. The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” he wrote.
“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always,” he wrote.
Lake Ontario has been called Lake Ontario since at least the 1600s, and it is the inspiration of the name for Canada’s most populous province, Ontario, which is home to Ottawa and Toronto.
Trump made a similar move last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” The Interior Department, Google and Apple complied with that directive, while the rest of the world largely has not.
Trump suggested Thursday other larger renamings could follow.
“So, the lake change, Lake of America, was something I’ve been thinking about for a long time. Actually, as you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico. We changed it, and now it’s very routinely the Gulf of America. So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake,” he said. “Now, all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”
Canadian maritime attorney Marc Isaacs told NBC News this week that a U.S. move on a name change of Lake Ontario wouldn’t affect other countries, including Canada, saying that no officials in either country own the naming rights to the lake.
“The Americans can call it whatever they want to call it,” Isaacs said. “It is Lake Ontario.”
Canadian Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly shrugged off Trump’s initial threats to change the name earlier this week.
“We’ll always call it Lake Ontario. Period,” she said. “We’re proud of our Great Lakes.”

sources.news_title: Trump Signs Order Renaming Lake Ontario
sources.text:
The Independent reports:
President Donald Trump has signed an order purporting to rename one of the five Great Lakes along the U.S.-Canada border in a fit of pique over his ongoing trade war with Ottawa that appears to have no end in sight.
Trump on Thursday signed an order directing federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America” in all official documents and records, echoing a smilier move from early in his second term when he attempted to unilaterally rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.”
“The Canadian officials have treated us very badly — they’re nasty people,” he said. Trump then suggested that Canada was “the worst to deal with on trade” despite the country’s long relationship with the U.S. and the trade agreement his administration negotiated during his first term. He complained that Canadians “feel entitled” and added that “we can’t have that.”
Read the full article.

sources.news_title: Trump signs executive order to change Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’
sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday afternoon to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” further needling Canada as he engages in a tense trade war with the United States’ northern ally.
Flanked in the Oval Office by large maps of the Great Lakes — one titled “Making the Great Lakes Even Greater,” with a “Lake America” label over Lake Ontario — Trump said the name change would be “effective immediately.”
“‘Lake of America’ was something I’ve been thinking about for a long time,” Trump said. “We have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”
Trump has wide latitude over how the US government refers to geographic landmarks, though he can’t force other countries to follow suit. After he took similar executive action last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America,” Mexican officials lambasted the move and made clear they would keep using the old moniker. Google later announced that its maps feature would reflect the name “Gulf of America” for American users, while Mexican users would still see the name Gulf of Mexico.
Trump had been floating the name change since trade talks between the US and Canada fell apart last week. Trump enacted 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend, and Canada quickly followed suit by announcing increased tariffs on various US products. Trump has threatened to further escalate if Canada doesn’t back down.
On Tuesday, Trump said he was seriously considering renaming Lake Ontario “in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer.” Canada is the United States’ second largest trading partner, behind Mexico, according to US Census data, making up 12.6% of its total trade.
It didn’t take Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney long to push back, pointing out in a post on X Thursday afternoon that the origin of Lake Ontario’s name is more than 400 years old, predating the founding of both the US and Canada. He concluded that his country would “forever” call it Lake Ontario.
“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,’” he wrote. “We know that the United States is changing. Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario — today and forever.”
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has been outspoken against Trump’s tariffs threats, echoed the Canadian prime minister’s comments. “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever,” he wrote in a social media post.
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston had a more succinct reaction on X shortly after Trump signed the executive order: “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy.”
The new executive order tasks Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and the Board on Geographic Names to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” within 30 days, including updating the Geographic Names Information System and removing “all references to Lake Ontario, consistent with applicable law.”
Trump also directed the Board on Geographic Names to provide guidance on the name change within the federal government, so agency maps, contracts, documents and communications state “Lake America” instead.
The director of the US Geological Survey said later Thursday, in a message the White House posted on X, that the agency has now designated the name change in all official USGS electronic documents. The change in printed documents will happen over the next several days.
In his executive order, Trump claims the name change reflects the fact that “the deepest parts of the Lake’s waters” and most of its “volume” are in US territory. He called the body of water — which borders Ontario, Canada and New York — “a tremendous asset to the United States and part of our Nation’s heritage.”
In the Oval Office Thursday, Trump repeatedly said Canada was the “worst to deal with on trade,” calling them “entitled.”
“The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people,” he said.
Shortly before Trump signed the executive order, GOP Sen. Susan Collins of Maine said on X that Canada had made a “good faith” decision to pull seafood and fish products from its retaliatory tariffs list. She urged Trump administration officials to respond “by returning to the negotiating table and working to amicably resolve this trade dispute.” Minutes later, images of Trump alongside the “Lake America” maps were broadcast live.
Collins is a top Democratic target in the midterm election, and the tariffs will be acutely felt in her home state.
The US-Canada trade talks seem to be on hold for now. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Wednesday that he’s not in active talks with his Canadian counterpart, Dominic LeBlanc.
“I would say we don’t have open channels right now. I have a good relationship with Minister LeBlanc, but right now I think the Canadian side is, you know, talking about their next steps,” Greer told CBC News in an interview from the White House North Lawn.
Fights over the name change may not be limited to Canada. After the president signed the executive order establishing the “Gulf of America,” the Associated Press — which shares writing style guidelines widely used by news organizations — refused to recognize the new name. The White House subsequently barred AP’s access to covering certain events in the Oval Office or traveling on Air Force One.
A federal judge ultimately ruled that the White House’s actions were unconstitutional.
This story has been updated with additional information and context.

sources.news_title: Trump Renames Lake Ontario, Fights Canada on Trade, and Rallies in Texas
sources.text:
Donald Trump is making major headlines with another bold geographic move. On Thursday, he signed an executive order targeting Lake Ontario. The order directs federal agencies to call the body of water Lake America. Trump argued the country should not honor a Canadian province during trade disputes. This action mirrors his earlier decision regarding the Gulf of Mexico. However, the Great Lake is shared between New York and Canada. Canadian officials quickly pushed back against the presidential decree. They noted American orders do not change international maps or Canadian law. Local residents on both sides of the border expressed strong reactions. Many Canadian leaders dismissed the proposed name as political theater.
The renaming comes amid an escalating trade war between the neighboring countries. Trade negotiations between Washington and Ottawa collapsed after tense discussions. Trump quickly imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian goods. He also threatened new tariffs on vehicles, auto parts, and steel. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded with retaliatory measures. Carney stated that American demands would destroy key Canadian industries. Ontario Premier Doug Ford urged both sides to return to the negotiating table. The standoff threatens supply chains across the northern border. Businesses on both sides worry about rising consumer costs and economic damage. Cross-border commerce faces its most serious disruption in decades.
Foreign policy challenges extend well beyond North American borders. The Trump administration is also ramping up severe economic pressure on Iran. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced aggressive new sanctions on the Iranian regime. Washington warned foreign countries to sever financial ties with Iran immediately. Trump described the strategy as an economic reckoning designed to isolate Tehran. The move follows ongoing military tensions and disputes over regional security. Allies and adversaries alike are closely watching the situation in the Middle East. Global energy markets continue to react to the heightened geopolitical friction. The administration insists that maximum pressure will deter hostile actions.
Meanwhile, Trump is turning his attention to domestic midterm politics. He is traveling to Texas to campaign for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton. Paxton secured the nomination after defeating veteran senator John Cornyn. Trump’s endorsement played a critical role in Paxton’s primary victory. Paxton now faces Democratic candidate James Talarico in the general election. Recent polls suggest the Texas Senate race is a competitive toss-up. Paxton has focused his campaign on energy independence and border protection. At the same time, Talarico has built substantial fundraising momentum statewide. Trump’s rally aims to energize conservative voters in the Lone Star State. The outcome could determine control of the United States Senate.
These simultaneous events highlight Trump’s combative and dynamic political approach. He consistently blends sharp trade battles with symbolic cultural fights. At home, he works tirelessly to maintain his grip on the Republican Party. Abroad, he uses economic levers to challenge longstanding trade and diplomatic norms. Whether altering lake names or rallying in Texas, Trump remains the center of attention. Voters will soon decide how these aggressive strategies impact the country. The upcoming midterm elections will serve as a crucial test for his entire agenda.

sources.news_title: Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America"
sources.text:
Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America"
Washington — President Trump on Thursday signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America," making good on a threat he made on social media earlier this week.
"We're going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario, effective immediately, to Lake America," the president said before he signed the order.
On Truth Social, the president said this week that the U.S. was giving "serious consideration" to changing the name and posted a map that crossed out the label "Lake Ontario." He also said the U.S. doesn't expect to be "doing much business with Ontario any longer." The announcement in the Oval Office Thursday is the president's latest move amid his trade war with Canada.
The order directs Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to update the Geographic Names Information System to reflect the name change. The GNIS works with the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to standardize geographic names for federal use. The president can't force other countries or international bodies to call it "Lake America," but he can require the federal government to do so.
Mr. Trump later posted to Truth Social a letter from the director of the U.S. Geological Survey announcing that the change had been made and "will begin occurring in printed documents over the next several days."
The president was asked what message he's sending to Canada with this executive order.
"No message," he said, but added, "As you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very, very sadly. Even the military. You know, we defend Canada for nothing."
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Lake Ontario is much older than the Declaration of Independence, and "naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario."
"The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word 'Ontari'io,' which, appropriately, means, 'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,'" Carney said. "The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always."
In New York, the only U.S. state that borders the lake, Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul said, "New York won't be calling it that."
On Saturday, 50% tariffs on some Canadian imports like wine and dairy kicked in, and on Monday, the president announced 50% tariffs on all Canadian steel and automotive imports starting in January.
In response, Carney announced that starting Sept. 8, Canada will begin imposing matching tariffs of up to 50% on billions of dollars of U.S. goods.
Mr. Trump also sought to change North America's highest mountain peak, Denali in Alaska, back to Mount McKinley. Although the federal government can't force other countries or private businesses to recognize the GNIS, when Mr. Trump sought to change the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America," some private entities adopted the new name.
Still, the White House punished The Associated Press after it declined to use "Gulf of America," restricting its reporters' access to White House and presidential spaces available to other news outlets.
On Thursday, Mr. Trump threatened to rename an ocean, too.
"Now all we need is an ocean," he said. "So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and — or — the Pacific."

sources.news_title: Trump signs order to 'immediately' rename Lake Ontario as Canada tensions erupt
sources.text:
Trump signs order to 'immediately' rename Lake Ontario as Canada tensions explode
Donald Trump's order directs federal agencies to refer to the lake shared with Canada with a new name.
Donald Trump has signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario, as the trade war with Canada continues. Amid strained relations with Canada, the US President said he signed an executive order on Thursday, renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.
The 80-year-old US leader said the change would take effect immediately. “We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario, effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump said in the Oval Office before signing the executive order. The change will apply only to the US, as President Trump cannot force Canada to follow his direction.
In recent days, Mr Trump had repeatedly threatened to take the symbolic step, although it was initially unclear whether he was serious about following through.
Following the move, a reporter quizzed Trump on what message he was trying to send, to which the US leader replied: "No message".
But he immediately added: “Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade.”
“They don’t pay for anything, and they want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state,” added MrTrump.
Such comments from the US President are reminiscent of his decision to order the US Government to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the ‘Gulf of America’.
The USGS now uses Gulf of America in its official US place-name database. However, the new name hasn't been universally adopted worldwide, with Mexico and other countries continuing to use the Gulf of Mexico.
His remarks capped a tumultuous week in US-Canada relations, marked by them being locked in an escalating trade war after talks collapsed last week.
Tariff hikes on steel, cars and car parts were announced by Mr Trump on Monday, due to be introduced in January.
Canada announced it would impose new tariffs on US goods earlier this week.
Tariffs, which are taxes imposed on goods imported from other countries, have been a central element of Mr Trump’s trade policy.
On Saturday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney blasted Mr Trump and said that a fresh wave of US tariffs on Canada is a "miscalculation". Mr Carney said that the tariffs were designed to "hurt and divide us", after trade talks broke down late on Friday.

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said Thursday he is renaming Lake Ontario to be known as "Lake America" in the United States as he exacerbates his trade war with Canada.
The Republican president signed an executive order that updated the lake's name for the U.S. geographic naming service. Trump cannot force Canada to follow his preferred naming convention, however.
The move is reminiscent of his move last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America.'"
Trump, who signed the order as he was sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, had a large sign behind him propped on a stand with a map of the Great Lakes. Over Lake Ontario, in big red letters, the map read "Lake America."
He told reporters that Canada is "the worst" to deal with on trade. "They feel entitled and we can't have that," he said.
The president has been floating the idea of the name change in recent days as the U.S. announced it was imposing 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down. Trump has been needling America's northern neighbor since he returned to the White House last year, suggesting the ally with whom the U.S. once had warm relations should instead be absorbed as the 51st state.
The U.S. and Canada share borders along multiple Great Lakes, including Lake Ontario.
The official U.S.-Canada border stretches across the water between Lake Ontario's northern and southern shores. The body of water forms much of New York State's coastline and separates Buffalo from Toronto, the capital of the province of Ontario. Toronto is Canada's most populous city and Ontario its most populous province.
Ontario is also the single largest export destination for more than a dozen U.S. states.
The lake's name comes from the Huron Indigenous people's word "oniatarí:io," which means "lake of shining waters," and it predates European settlement in the region. The province, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
The International Hydrographic Organization — of which both the United States and Canada are members — works to ensure that the world's seas, oceans and navigable waters are surveyed and charted uniformly, and also names some of them. But there is no single international body that determines names of international bodies of water.
