sources.news_title: Honoring the American History of the Great Lakes and Renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America
sources.text:
HONORING THE AMERICAN HISTORY OF THE GREAT LAKES AND RENAMING LAKE ONTARIO AS LAKE AMERICA
By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered:
Section 1. Purpose and Policy. As I announced in Executive Order 14172 of January 20, 2025 (Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness), it is the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements. The United States is the greatest protector of the Great Lakes, including the body of water currently known as Lake Ontario. Without the security and investment provided by the United States, this freshwater system would not be open for shipping, recreation, and responsible use to the same extent as it is today. The United States Coast Guard supplies 9 of the 11 ice breaking vessels on the Great Lakes, securing commercial shipping lanes free of charge. The United States has invested nearly $4 billion in protecting the Great Lakes freshwater ecosystem in the last decade, while Canada has invested far less in similar initiatives over the same period.
Sec. 2. Lake America. (a) The body of water currently known as Lake Ontario is a tremendous asset to the United States and part of our Nation’s heritage. With the deepest parts of the Lake’s waters lying within United States territory, the United States claims most of the Lake’s volume. The Lake has long been an integral asset to American exploration, settlement, commerce, and defense. From the colonial period through the early republic, the Lake served as a critical artery for American trade, commerce, and military logistics, including the establishment in Oswego of a historic fort and the first United States port of call from the St. Lawrence Seaway, shipbuilding and naval operations during the War of 1812 at Sackets Harbor and other New York posts, and the movement of goods, settlers, and later industrial cargoes that linked the interior of the United States to eastern markets and the Atlantic. Maritime commerce on the broader Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway system — of which the Lake is the easternmost and gateway segment — continues to generate substantial economic activity for the United States, supporting hundreds of thousands of American jobs and billions of dollars in annual economic output, cargo value, and related business revenue, with our ports, carriers, and States deriving a significant share of the system’s benefits in iron ore, limestone, coal, agricultural products, and other bulk commodities. Water from the Lake is used to supply nuclear, natural gas, and oil-fired power plants and to supply municipal drinking water to nearby communities. United States domestic and cross-border shipping activity on the Great Lakes system has historically underpinned regional manufacturing, steel production, agriculture, and energy supply chains in several States, reflecting the strategic and economic importance of these waters to the United States that continues to this day. The Lake will continue to play a pivotal role in shaping America’s future and the global economy. In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation’s economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America.
(b) Within 30 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of the Interior (Secretary) shall, in coordination with the Board on Geographic Names and consistent with 43 U.S.C. 364 through 364f, take all appropriate actions to rename as “Lake America” the body of water currently named as Lake Ontario, bounded on the south and east by the State of New York, and on the north, west, and southwest by the Canadian province of Ontario. The Secretary, conjointly with the Board on Geographic Names, shall subsequently update the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) to reflect the renaming of the Lake and remove all references to Lake Ontario from the GNIS, consistent with applicable law. The Board on Geographic Names shall provide guidance to ensure all Federal Government references to Lake Ontario, including on executive department and agency maps, contracts, and other documents and communications, shall reflect its renaming.
Sec. 3. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this order shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect:
(i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or the head thereof; or
(ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
(b) This order shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations.
(c) This order is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any other person.
(d) The costs for publication of this order shall be borne by the Department of the Interior.
DONALD J. TRUMP
THE WHITE HOUSE,
August 27, 2026.

sources.news_title: Trump Orders Lake Ontario Renamed Lake America in Canada Feud
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Trump on Thursday signed documents directing that Lake Ontario be renamed “Lake America,” a move that comes as his tariff-fueled trade dispute with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney intensifies.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario, effective immediately, to Lake America,” Trump told reporters from the Oval Office.
“We filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else. We notified all of the various people that we have to notify. So we’ve done everything that you have to do, and this is official, effective immediately,” he said.
Trump blamed Canadian officials for the worsening tensions, saying they had handled the situation “very badly.” He added, “They’re nasty people. They charge our farmers 400% tariffs.”
The president previously moved to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” last year.
“If you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” Trump said Thursday.

Civics buffs ‘shame’ Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ — 8:19 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America, civics buffs on the internet were quick to point out how it would change one of their childhood geography lessons.
Students are taught that one way to remember the names of the Great Lakes is to use the mnemonic H-O-M-E-S, which stands for Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior.
Now, they say, taking out Ontario and adding America would change the acronym to S-H-A-M-E.
Ontario premier rejects ‘Lake America’ days after clash with Trump — 6:23 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Ontario Premier Doug Ford rejected President Donald Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America,” writing on social media: “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.”
Ford told The Associated Press earlier this week that Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” and “disgusted with President Trump” over Trump’s tariff policies and his departure from Reagan’s free-trade legacy. Trump, in turn, dismissed Ford’s comments as “bluster,” called him Carney’s “flunky” and mocked him as the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother” of the late Toronto Mayor Rob Ford.
Trump’s renaming order came days after that exchange, raising the possibility that the move was also aimed at the Ontario premier.
Trump uses infamous ‘Mission Accomplished’ phrase to declare victory in Iran war that’s still ongoing — 5:49 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The president is reviving the phrase that came to haunt George W. Bush in Iraq — to claim success in Iran.
The president posted on his social media site depicting himself over images of American flags, an aircraft carrier and jets, as well as a frowning Bush next to a sign reading “Mission Not Accomplished: 2001-2021.”
The post also shows Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed by strikes in February, next to a sign reading “Mission Accomplished 2026.”
Bush stood on an aircraft carrier under a “Mission Accomplished” banner just six weeks into an Iraq war that dragged on for years, a move that came to be seen as a political blunder.
Trump’s latest post also ignores that Trump himself was president for the four years of his first term during the time his post implies U.S. military failure.
Despite the president’s insistence, the war in Iran has continued, with no end in sight.
Stars and Stripes staffers sue Pentagon to challenge their firings — 5:38 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Three staff members from the Stars and Stripes military news outlet are suing to challenge their recent firings by the Pentagon, accusing the Trump administration of violating their First Amendment free speech rights to speak out against government interference in their work.
Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin and Middle East reporter Lara Korte are named as plaintiffs in the federal lawsuit filed Thursday in Washington, D.C.
The Pentagon, which partially funds the news outlet, fired them last week. A Pentagon spokesperson declined to comment on the lawsuit’s allegations.
Slavin says he was dismissed for insubordination after giving an interview in which he objected to potential censorship by the U.S. military. Korte participated in the same interview. Lederer was dismissed shortly after announcing his impending retirement.
Carney rejects Trump’s ‘Lake America’ renaming with a swipe at a changing US — 4:16 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” invoking the lake’s Indigenous roots while pointedly casting the episode as part of a transformation of the United States under Trump.
In a social media post, Carney noted that Lake Ontario takes its name from the Wendat word “Ontari’io,” meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,” and said the name predates both the Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence.
“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” Carney said.
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”
Judge questions why Kennedy Center is moving so quickly to return Trump’s name to building — 4:14 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Just seconds after the Trump administration’s lawyer, Bradley Mayers, began making his case at a nearly two-hour hearing, U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper interrupted to ask why the Kennedy Center needed to begin inscribing the president’s name on the institution’s facade as soon as Sept. 8.
“What’s magic about that date?” Cooper asked, quipping that sometimes judges travel over the Labor Day holiday.
Mayers responded that the timeline was in accordance with a vote earlier this month by the Trump-aligned board. As he returned to his arguments that renovations at the Kennedy Center require energy and talent, Cooper interjected again.
“That’s all fine and good,” the judge said. “What does that have to do with what Congress intended in these statutes? That’s really what’s before me.”
Canadian historian says ‘Lake America’ move should be mocked, warns of backlash — 4:00 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Canadian historian Robert Bothwell says Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” should be met with ridicule.
“People should be standing around the capital laughing themselves sick,” Bothwell said. “Everybody knows the Gulf of America is a joke, and this is a joke in an awful way.”
Bothwell says the renaming fits what he sees as Trump’s broader effort to subordinate Canada and said it makes a negotiated settlement between the two countries “next to impossible.
He also warned that if Apple or Google adopt “Lake America” on their maps, it could provoke a backlash in Canada.
“It’s an insult,” Bothwell said, adding that Canadians could respond with boycotts that might grow into a broader political movement.
DOJ sues 4 more states for offering in-state tuition for immigrant students — 3:03 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The U.S. Department of Justice is suing four states that provide in-state tuition for students without legal status, saying the practice discriminates against U.S. citizens and encourages illegal immigration.
The complaints against Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon and Washington were filed Thursday, marking just the latest legal challenges over tuition breaks for such students. In all, the department has filed 21 lawsuits, with five of those resulting in judges permanently enjoining and declaring unconstitutional laws that gave reduced tuition to students living in the U.S. illegally.
“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said in a statement. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”
Federal prosecutors are seeking to keep the four states from providing in-state tuition rates for all immigrants who maintain in-state residency, regardless of whether those students are lawfully present in the United States.
Democratic-led states, including Mass., sue Trump administration over changes to family planning program — 2:56 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The program provides grants to health care providers for contraception, cancer screenings and other services, mainly for low-income women.
More than 20 states, including New York, Massachusetts and California, argue in a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services that the department broke the law when it set stricter rules this year for which providers qualify for the program, including requiring them to end diversity programs.
“This lawsuit is about ensuring safe and effective family planning and reproductive care remains accessible to all,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said at a news conference, adding that the new requirements were politically motivated.
New analysis says the Trump administration’s logic used to cut emissions rules is flawed — 2:44 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The Trump administration relied on flawed logic to justify scrapping vehicle emissions standards earlier this year, according to a new study by a group of economists published Thursday in the journal Science.
It scrapped the emissions standards when it revoked the endangerment finding, which had long served as the legal underpinning for federal regulation of greenhouse gas emissions.
Researchers who examined the Environmental Protection Agency’s analysis for doing so said eliminating the rules will cost the country billions of dollars, not save it billions.
Even setting aside environmental reasons for keeping emissions rules, “the economic case for the rollback of the standards still falls apart,” said Antonio Bento, one of the study’s authors.
The EPA said it stands by its economic analysis.
“We will not attempt to push an EV mandate on the American people based on facially implausible projections,” the agency said in a statement.
Senator Markey, who questioned Kennedy about his 2019 Samoa trip, says the now-health secretary lied — 2:34 p.m.
By the Associated Press
During Kennedy’s confirmation hearings to be the nation’s health secretary, Sen. Edward Markey, D-Mass., asked about Kennedy’s 2019 trip to Samoa at least three times.
Again and again, Kennedy denied that his reason for the trip was related to vaccines.
Markey said new documents published by the AP and The Guardian on Thursday “confirm what we already knew: RFK Jr. lied to Congress.”
“This is a pattern, not a slip,” Markey said in a statement. “He should never have been confirmed, and he cannot be trusted to run HHS for even one more day.”
In response to questions from the AP, the Department of Health and Human Services said that the Samoa visit “was unrelated to vaccines.”
The US president can’t dictate what the rest of the world calls it — 2:31 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Trump has wide latitude over how the U.S. government recognizes geographic places and landmarks.
But he can’t force Canada or individual citizens on either side of the border to follow his preferred naming conventions.
Trump introduced idea to rename Lake Ontario hours before Canada announced its reciprocal tariffs — 2:29 p.m.
By the Associated Press
“The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer,” Trump posted Tuesday on Truth Social.
This latest branding move — reminiscent of his move to rechristen the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” — highlights how much Trump’s rhetoric and trade policy have sundered the previously warm relationship between Washington and Ottawa.
In a scheduled announcement hours after Trump’s post, Canadian leaders unveiled tariffs on about $20 billion worth of American goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment — a retaliation for the Trump administration’s new 50% tariffs on Canadian goods.
Lake Ontario’s name predates either country — 2:26 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The lake’s name comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” meaning “lake of shining waters,” and predates European settlement in the region. The province, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
The International Hydrographic Organization — of which both the United States and Canada are members — works to ensure that the world’s seas, oceans and navigable waters are surveyed and charted uniformly, and also names some of them. But there is no single international body that determines the names of international bodies of water.
Lutnick downplays potential of demolishing Kennedy Center — 2:21 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Trump administration lawyers raised the prospect earlier this week that the Kennedy Center would be demolished if Trump’s name wasn’t recognized at the institution to facilitate further fundraising for renovations.
“What was pointed out,” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told reporters, “was that if you do nothing, bad things happen. But they’re not going to happen on Thursday.”
Lutnick was speaking ahead of a hearing in Washington to consider arguments over the Kennedy Center’s move to inscribe Trump’s name on the building. He argued that the effort was a way to recognize the president’s contributions to the renovations and said the board wasn’t trying to rename the institution, which a judge ruled earlier this year was illegal.
“That’s yesterday,” Lutnick said of the renaming debate.
Trump sidesteps question about CIA director’s Russia trip — 2:18 p.m.
By the Associated Press
CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise visit to Moscow earlier this week, but Trump won’t share what he told Russian officials.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing unidentified people briefed on the matter, that Ratcliffe’s trip was to deliver a warning to Russia not to attack NATO countries.
Asked during Thursday’s Oval Office exchange with reporters about whether Ratcliffe delivered that message to Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump offered a roundabout response.
“I don’t want to comment on that, but they’re not going to attack,” Trump said.
Trump says US is sending aid to Nepal after catastrophic floods — 2:13 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The president said recent flooding in a border area of China and Nepal was terrible to see, describing how “strong, well-built buildings were wiped out like they were toothpicks.”
Talking to reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday, he said the U.S. has spoken with Nepalese leaders and offered to provide “anything they want.”
Trump said there were 50 or 60 Americans in the area but added that a full accounting hasn’t been completed.
The State Department has said 90 Americans were unaccounted for in China and Nepal. It said it was not aware of any U.S. deaths.
Trump calls Cruz ‘very talented,’ says the Texas senator ‘might’ run for president in 2028 — 2:04 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The president was asked about Cruz teasing a 2028 presidential run and responded, “I would say that he’s very talented. He’s a very good friend of mine. I think he might do that, yeah.”
Trump added of Cruz: “He’s a talented guy.”
Cruz ran for president in 2016 and was among the last Republican primary candidates still in the race when Trump clinched the party’s nomination.

By the Associated Press
AP’s latest findings about Robert F. Kennedy Jr.‘s trip to Samoa show his platform “is built on lies and grifts that leave a trail of dead children in their wake,” said Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, which oversees Kennedy’s health department.
The AP reported earlier Thursday that new documents refute Kennedy’s account that his 2019 visit, before a deadly measles outbreak, had “nothing to do with vaccines.”
Responding to the reporting, Wyden said he plans to press Republicans to refer Kennedy to the Justice Department for criminal investigation for lying to Congress.
If Democrats take the Senate majority in this fall’s elections, he added, his committee will prioritize holding Kennedy accountable.
“There are consequences for lying to Congress,” he said.
Group of Democratic senators calls on ICE to cancel plan for shock gloves — 12:30 p.m.
By the Associated Press
A group of U.S. senators led by Democrat Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada is urging Immigration and Customs Enforcement to cancel its plan to outfit officers with gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks.
In a letter to ICE’s acting director, Cortez Masto and 15 of her colleagues in the Democratic caucus questioned ICE’s need to spend up to $20 million on the devices and the agency’s ability to use them appropriately.
“The blatant and tragic misuse of force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, Houston, Maine, and other locations around the country raises significant skepticism about the agency’s professional capability to safely deploy a new tool that could be used to harm Americans without cause,” the letter said.
The shortage illustrates the cascading fallout from Trump’s decision to launch a war against Iran — 11:50 a.m.
By the Associated Press
U.S. missile stocks in Europe have been moved to the Middle East, where U.S. and Gulf allies have fired off significant numbers of interceptors, including Patriots, to thwart Iran’s drones and missiles. Some of those attacks have killed and wounded American troops.
Though a Russian ballistic missile attack against NATO countries is not imminently expected, CIA Director John Ratcliffe went to Moscow this week to warn Russia not to attack, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump played down the significance of the rare and secretive trip, saying it was “sort of semi-routine.”
European and NATO officials say Russia could be in a position to attack countries in the alliance by 2030. Patriot stockpiles are projected to rebound by then. In the meantime, Russia’s war in Ukraine could hinder its ability to carry out any missile attack on Europe as it would be a challenge for Moscow to fight an air war on two fronts.
US Patriot missile stocks in Europe are ‘beyond critical’ due to Iran war, officials say — 11:47 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The shortage of advanced missile interceptors is largely driven by Trump’s war with Iran, a U.S. defense official in Europe and a NATO official told The Associated Press, raising concerns about vulnerabilities in NATO countries to a potential Russian attack.
The U.S. defense official said the most concerning shortfall involves Patriot missile interceptors, which can shoot down Russia’s high-speed ballistic missiles. The NATO official confirmed the low inventories of Patriots among American and NATO forces in Europe. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.
In the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault on, for example, a military headquarters or power plant, NATO could be in a similar position to Patriot-starved Ukraine and be forced “to take punch after punch in the mouth,” the U.S. defense official said.
In Europe, the American military “definitely” does not have enough Patriots to stop any possible sustained ballistic missile attack and would have “very limited” capability to defend against a single ballistic missile strike or a stray Russian missile that goes off course, the U.S. official said.
Michigan Democrats want to fight Trump. First they have to stop fighting each other — 11:40 a.m.
By the Associated Press
When Democrats gathered this week in a West Michigan congressional district they’re trying to flip blue, they wanted to talk about the cost of living under President Donald Trump. But it didn’t take long for the conversation to turn to a controversy dividing their party.
One attendee chided U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten for failing to support Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
“Your inflammatory rhetoric has nothing to do with creating a better economic future for the people of West Michigan, and everything to do with protecting the pipeline of our tax dollars to Israel,” the woman said.
The exchange captured a problem confronting Democrats as they head toward November. Party leaders believe concerns about the economy have given them an opening to win control of Congress, but internal divisions are making it harder to keep the focus there.
New sanctions and a trade embargo leave Iran with few places to turn — 11:35 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Iran’s economy, already strained by high inflation, years of Western sanctions and a war that has sharply reduced oil revenue, is poised for more instability as the Trump administration tries to coerce other countries into ending all financial dealings with the Islamic Republic.
A decision by the United Arab Emirates to suspend trade relations with Iran last week kick-started the White House’s latest attempt to isolate Tehran into submission. Iran entered the war with its foreign commerce concentrated among a relatively small group of countries, leaving it with fewer places to turn now.
The success of the U.S. strategy will largely hinge on China, the main buyer of Iranian oil and its top trading partner. Russia, a fellow target of sweeping U.S.-led sanctions, has a military conflict and economic crisis of its own and probably can’t offer longtime ally Iran much hard financial support.
Canada is bolstering its defense industry as US relations fray — 11:30 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The Canadian government is investing an additional $60 billion over the next five years to reduce its dependence on American suppliers, a shift due to Trump’s pressure to contribute more to NATO as well as strained trade relations with Washington.
Canada aims to boost domestic defense capabilities and create jobs while developing innovative technologies for military and civilian use, like drones and robotics. Clothing maker Wuxly, known for luxury parkas, is joining in, making high-tech military gear.
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s vow to strengthen Canadian economic self-sufficiency is a boon for Canadian startups and established companies as well as firms in Europe.
UEFA has also gone to court in Florida against FIFA — 11:05 a.m.
By the Associated Press
UEFA also filed a request in a southern Florida district for authorization of discovery “in a foreign proceeding” against FIFA itself, which has offices in the Miami suburb of Coral Gables.
Thrive and Kushner were to be the anchor investors intending to pay FIFA $4.2 billion for a 20% stake in a subsidiary that would run the soccer body’s commercial events, including the World Cup.
A 56-page UEFA document seen by The Associated Press suggests the $4.2 billion could have been a “fraudulently off-market price promoted by Infantino for his own benefit.”
Infantino dropped the sell-off plan on Aug. 1 after a furious backlash by global soccer leaders, including UEFA.
Europe’s soccer body seeks evidence from Kushner fund for criminal complaint against FIFA’s Infantino — 10:55 a.m.
By the Associated Press
UEFA is preparing a criminal complaint against FIFA President Gianni Infantino in Swiss courts for possible financial mismanagement over his failed plan to sell future World Cup profits to private investors.
UEFA said Thursday it filed documents in a Manhattan court requesting discovery of potential evidence from the New York investment fund, Thrive Capital Management, founded by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Iran thanks China as it dismisses Trump’s D-Day sanctions threat — 10:50 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Iran’s top negotiator and parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf is thanking China for rejecting the U.S. “economic D-Day” policies against Iran.
“We welcome China’s principled statement rejecting illegal sanctions against Iran,” Qalibaf posted on social media Wednesday.
Earlier this week, Tehran had warned that it would respond harshly to expanded U.S. sanctions, including measures against countries it sees as cooperating with Washington. Iran has repeatedly targeted Bahrain and other Gulf countries with missiles and drones since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28.
Another tanker is reported struck in the Strait of Hormuz — 10:45 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said Thursday that it had received a report of an oil tanker hit in the Strait of Hormuz.
The monitoring agency, run by the British military, said that local authorities reported that the vessel was hit by an unknown projectile on Tuesday in the waters between Oman and Iran, causing it to catch fire.
The crew was reported to be safe and there have been no reports of environmental damage, the UKMTO said.
Canadian official says US has dropped objections to Canada’s cultural programs — 10:20 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The message from Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc suggests that by dropping objections to Canada’s efforts to promote French language and Canadian culture, the U.S. side has created some room for compromise in the trade standoff.
LeBlanc wrote on X Thursday that the measures “will not be subject to future U.S. trade actions,” and that he looks forward to “constructive U.S. clarifications’’ that could “create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement.’’
Speaking to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation Wednesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the U.S. has had some “questions’’ about whether the cultural programs put U.S. companies at a disadvantage, but said the U.S. “recognizes the importance and sensitivity of the French language’’ to Canada. “There is no way we would let a good deal go by for something like this,” Greer added.
Qatari leader went to Tehran seeking an off-ramp from the war — 10:15 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani was in Tehran on Thursday trying diplomacy to resolve the Iran war.
Qatar’s foreign ministry said in a post on X that Al Thani and Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi discussed “the efforts being made to reduce escalation,” as well as a proposed plan between Iran and Oman to allow ships safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and clear the vital commercial waterway of dangerous mines.
Al Thani’s office said the prime minister emphasized the “necessity of respecting the sovereignty of neighboring countries and the freedom of navigation” on the strait.
Al Thani also met Thursday with Iran’s parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf to review efforts to reduce escalation and resume dialogue, the Qatari government said.
New documents refuting RFK Jr testimony were obtained through an open records lawsuit — 10:00 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The letters featured in the AP’s Thursday story about Kennedy’s 2019 trip to Samoa had been included in emails in State Department records.
The department released them to the AP and The Guardian as the result of an open records lawsuit brought with the aid of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. The letters, shared recently, were among hundreds of pages of documents released over a period of months.
Based on other emails released as part of the lawsuit, the AP and the Guardian reported in February that officials with the State Department and UNICEF privately discussed that the trip was about vaccines.
HHS responds to AP report on Kennedy’s letter about measles vaccine — 9:30 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The Department of Health and Human Services said in response to questions from the AP that the Samoa visit “was unrelated to vaccines.”
“Any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory,” the department said in a written statement.
Kennedy was not under oath during his confirmation hearing. Knowingly giving material false testimony to Congress is a crime that carries a possible prison sentence regardless of whether a person is under oath, though it is rarely prosecuted.
HHS did not make Kennedy available for an interview. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. The Samoan prime minister’s office and the former prime minister who corresponded with Kennedy did not respond to requests for comment. Neither did Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine nonprofit Kennedy led.
AP exclusive: RFK Jr. said a Samoa trip had nothing to do with vaccines. New documents refute that — 9:29 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. repeatedly told lawmakers who held the key to his confirmation last year that his 2019 visit to Samoa before a deadly measles outbreak had “ nothing to do with vaccines.” New documents obtained by The Associated Press and The Guardian refute that testimony.
Kennedy, then a prominent anti-vaccine activist, preceded the visit with a letter to the Samoan prime minister requesting to study the Pacific island nation’s measles, mumps and rubella vaccines after the deaths of two children who had received them. In the letter, he used the words vaccine or vaccination eight times.
The letter raises questions about how truthful Kennedy was in testimony before Congress. During an arduous confirmation process where he needed the support of some skeptical Republican lawmakers to advance, Kennedy also pledged to maintain vaccine policies that, once in office, he moved to change.
Outgoing White House press secretary talks Texas and her replacement — 9:05 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Karoline Leavitt says there’s “no shortage of applications” to replace her.
“I’ve given my advice to the president on what he should look for, and I’ll continue to do that until he makes a decision,” she told “Fox and Friends” on Thursday that the pick needs to be someone Trump “trusts fully.”
In what Fox hosts billed as her last official interview on the network, Leavitt teased a trip Trump is taking to Houston Thursday evening to attend a Republican National Committee fundraiser in support of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign. Trump will visit NASA’s Johnson Space Center on Friday.
White House says some Americans have been rescued from flooding in Nepal — 8:56 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The US has rescued a handful of Americans in the wake of devastating flooding in Nepal, outgoing White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in an interview on “Fox and Friends” on Thursday morning.
Leavitt said the US has offered its help to local authorities and will prioritize Americans in its response. “We’re focused on rescuing every American that we possibly can,” she said.
Rescue teams searched Thursday for hundreds of missing people along the Nepal-China border, where the collapse of a glacier sent a catastrophic and deadly torrent of water and mud several stories high sweeping through communities.
Videos of the disaster showed people running before the floodwaters swallowed them up. At least 353 people were killed, police said, and more than 1,300 are missing. Melting glaciers have become more common because of human-caused climate change.
The number of Americans applying for jobless aid slips to 203,000 as layoffs remain low — 8:47 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The Labor Department numbers released Thursday show layoffs are rare and most Americans enjoy job security, but that doesn’t point to a great job market for workers.
Scarred by the worker shortages that followed the COVID-19 pandemic, companies are reluctant to let go of staff. But they aren’t hiring much either. So times are tough for Americans seeking to break into the job market as well as people who lost their jobs and are looking for new work. Economists describe a “no hire, no fire″ job market.
So far this year, employers — companies, nonprofits and government agencies — have added an average 61,000 jobs a month. It’s better than the 9,700 they averaged last year as high interest rates and Trump’s erratic trade policies discouraged companies from hiring. But it’s well below historic hiring patterns.
ICE officer charged in Minneapolis shooting is released from Texas jail — 8:37 a.m.
By the Associated Press
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with shooting a man and lying about it during the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis was released from a Texas jail Thursday, after a judge refused to order his return to Minnesota.
Christian Castro was released from a detention center in Brownsville, Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Trevino said in an email.
A day earlier, US District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. wrote in an order that said he couldn’t prevent a county sheriff from releasing Castro or order Texas Governor Greg Abbott to sign his extradition warrant.
Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.
Minnesota officials believe Castro could flee to Mexico.
New Fed chair Kevin Warsh under pressure to clarify views on inflation, interest rates — 7:43 a.m.
By the Associated Press
New Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh has brought sharp change in how the central bank communicates by saying much less than his predecessors about the economy and inflation.
But so far, many economists and Wall Street investors haven’t been thrilled with that approach.
On Friday, Warsh has a high-stakes opportunity to address those concerns and underscore his inflation-fighting bona fides when he gives his speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, during the Fed’s annual economic symposium.
What many economists and Wall Street analysts are hoping for is a clear signal on how he thinks the Fed should handle the stubbornly elevated inflation that has caused pervasive gloom among many consumers. At his last press conference, he sowed confusion by ducking repeated questions on whether the Fed would hike its benchmark interest rate if inflation stays high.
After six months of Iran war, US goals have shifted. The Strait of Hormuz is now a top concern. — 7:22 a.m.
By the Associated Press
When Trump launched the war with Iran in late February, he initially forecast it would last four to five weeks. Six months later, there’s still no off-ramp in sight despite Trump’s repeated assertions that the war has been won or a deal to resolve it was nearly complete.
A June memorandum of understanding designed to pave the way to end the war has fallen by the wayside.
One of the prime goals now — reopening the Strait of Hormuz — was not one of Trump’s original objectives. The waterway had been a vital shipping lane through which about 20 percent of the world’s oil passed.
But Iran seized on it as a chokepoint for the global economy and it has been largely closed since the war started, driving up prices for fuel and fertilizer needed for farms and creating economic and political pressure in the US.
The US has had tactical success on its goals to degrade Iran’s military capabilities. But some of the other key objectives Trump laid out at the start of the conflict remain unfulfilled.
Judge denies Minnesota’s bid to compel the extradition of an ICE officer from Texas — 7:20 a.m.
By the Associated Press
A federal judge on Wednesday refused to order Texas to extradite an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with shooting a man and lying about it during the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis.
US District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. wrote in an order that he couldn’t prevent a county sheriff from releasing Christian Castro or order Texas Governor Greg Abbott to sign his extradition warrant.
The Cameron County sheriff said he would release Castro on Thursday morning.
Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.
After a Minnesota judge issued a nationwide warrant for Castro’s arrest in May, authorities, including Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, arrested Castro in Cameron County on May 29. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition since his arrest, but he remains in custody in Brownsville, Texas, a city bordering Mexico.
Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro must be released after 90 days of detention, which is Thursday.
Republicans face a midterm verdict as Iran war drags on months longer than Trump promised — 7:18 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The Iran war has reshaped the rapidly approaching midterm elections, undermining Trump’s campaign pledge to steer clear of foreign conflicts and challenging Republicans who would rather focus on their tax cuts as they cling to narrow majorities in Congress.
While the president’s supporters are undeterred, the war’s unpopularity and economic ripple effects could tilt the scales in tightly contested US House districts.
Midterm elections are always difficult for the party in power in Washington. But interviews with voters around the country show how a war that Trump expected to end with a swift victory could undermine the final years of his presidency.
About two-thirds of US adults say the war with Iran has not been worth fighting, according to a July poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. That includes the vast majority of Democrats and independents, as well as more than one-third of Republicans.
In Congress, Republicans have shifted from initially cheerleading Trump’s moves in Iran to expressing concern about the toll of the war.
Faltering diplomatic efforts to end Iran war continue — 7:15 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Pakistan said Thursday that it was continuing diplomatic efforts to help resolve the crisis between the United States and Iran, and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said at a news briefing that Field Marshal Asim Munir’s recent visit to Tehran was aimed at reviving the June memorandum of understanding to reopen the strait.
Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani is expected in Tehran on Thursday for talks with Iranian officials on “ways to de-escalate tensions & create the conditions conducive to dialogue,” Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said on X.
The discussions, confirmed by Tehran, will also address “freedom of navigation” in the Strait of Hormuz and the need to return to the prewar status quo, according to Majed Al Ansari, an agency spokesperson.
But President Trump told Al Jazeera by phone on Wednesday that he has “no time schedule” to wrap up the conflict that will reach the six-month mark on Friday. Trump told the Qatar-based broadcaster that he believes the United States is “winning very big.”

sources.news_title: Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
sources.text:
The federal minister overseeing talks with the United States has signalled a potential détente in the worsening trade war, suggesting that Canada was open to new negotiations after receiving what he described as clarifications from his American counterpart.
But that optimistic view from Dominic LeBlanc, who raised the prospect of a “mutually beneficial” trade deal on Thursday, less than a week after negotiations fell apart, was quickly derailed by U.S. President Donald Trump’s declaration that he was renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America.
The minister was responding to comments made a day earlier by his main negotiating partner, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who said that while the American side raised concerns about Canadian policies that urge online streaming companies to promote French programming, it did not insist on changes.
To First Nations that named Lake Ontario, Trump’s threat doesn’t hold water
“Canada welcomes that the U.S. is now withdrawing its positions on discoverability and labelling and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future U.S. trade actions,” Mr. LeBlanc said Thursday in a post on X.
“We look forward to further constructive U.S. clarifications on their other positions, which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty.”
Mr. Greer had made the comments in a Wednesday interview with CBC News, during which he acknowledged Canadian frustrations.
“Our view is, you know, don’t retaliate. But I know how people are feeling in Canada and what they think,” he said.
Mr. Trump did not maintain that tone during a Thursday afternoon White House news conference, where he signed an executive order next to a map showing Lake Ontario renamed as Lake America.
“This is official, effective immediately,” he said.
Last year, Mr. Trump declared that the U.S. was renaming the Gulf of Mexico, saying it was in the country’s national interest.
“We changed it, and now it’s very routinely called the Gulf of America. So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean. So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” he said.
During the news conference, Mr. Trump repeated some of his past grievances with Ottawa, including claims that Canada’s auto policies are unfair and that the country does not spend enough on its military.
“Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade,” he said.
On Mr. Trump’s lake renaming, Prime Minister Mark Carney responded with a post on X.
“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.’
“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Gulf of understanding: The way we see the Earth has never been set in stone
Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded with a social-media post: “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.”
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew dismissed the President’s announcement.
“You know when a rock band is really over the hill, and you see them in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago? I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” he told reporters in Winnipeg. “It’s not his best work.”
After trade negotiations collapsed late Friday, Mr. Trump approved 50-per-cent tariffs on about $28-billion worth of Canadian goods.
Ottawa responded by outlining on Tuesday countertariffs targeting nearly 900 American products that are scheduled to come into force Sept. 8. However, the Finance Department announced late Wednesday that it would be adjusting its planned tariffs after industry feedback.
— Finance Canada (@FinanceCanada) August 27, 2026
The changes included removing seafood and fish products from Canada’s list of countertariffs, while adding new items such as wood charcoal and copper wire.
Restaurants Canada, which represents the Canadian dining industry, welcomed Ottawa’s reversal on seafood tariffs, which would have driven up food costs.
After Canada walked away from the trade negotiations, Mr. Carney suggested Saturday morning that the Canadian side was receiving contradictory messages from the Americans.
He said the Canadian team, which included Mr. LeBlanc and chief negotiator Janice Charette, was unified.
“You could not say that about the United States administration,” he said.
Four takeaways from Canada’s tariff counterpunch
During that Saturday news conference, Mr. Carney said the American side made last-minute changes related to sovereignty, the French language and the treatment of large trucks that ultimately could not be supported.
In his interview this week, Mr. Greer rejected those characterizations.
Speaking in both English and French, he said there is “no way” that his side would have allowed the deal to fall apart over issues related to how streaming services promote French-language programs.
He said there are currently no “open channels” of communication between the two sides and suggested that the U.S. will respond if Canada follows through with its planned countertariffs. On Monday, Mr. Trump said he would double auto tariffs to 50 per cent from 25 per cent as of Jan. 1, 2027, and have them also apply to auto parts, which have so far been exempted.
Mr. Greer disputed Canada’s assertions that it was the U.S. side that brought new last-minute demands to the table. He said it was Canada that pushed for additional changes related to the treatment of the auto sector and large trucks.
The U.S. had offered to lower the tariff on Canadian automobiles to 15 per cent from 25 per cent, but the two sides disagreed about whether the reduction would also apply to medium and heavy-duty trucks.
Tariff relief for trucks is a key issue for Canada given that General Motors Co. produces the Chevrolet Silverado in Oshawa and Ford Motor Co. is spending billions to retool its plant in Oakville to produce F-Series trucks.
The Globe and Mail has reported that there were disagreements within the Trump administration about how hard to push Canada on metal tariffs, which played a role in derailing the negotiations at the last minute. U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick demanded that certain products made of aluminum not be included in the tariff reductions.
Speaking to reporters in Washington on Thursday, Mr. Lutnick said the words “medium and heavy trucks” were only raised by Canada last Friday at 4 p.m., hours before negotiations ultimately fell apart.
“I met with LeBlanc 10 times. I spoke to Carney twice. These were not raised. These were not part of it,” he said.
Mr. Lutnick also said that the U.S. was not pushing for limitations on the French language in Canada.
“Do I care about how the Québécois speak? I mean, what could matter less to America? We don’t care,” he said, claiming that Mr. Carney had “manufactured” the language issue.
“Canada made the decision for political purposes. They wanted to walk away. This is politics only,” Mr. Lutnick said, predicting that Canada’s tone will change after Quebec’s provincial election and Alberta’s referendum on whether to remain in Canada or to hold a second, binding vote on sovereignty. Both the referendum and the Quebec election are set for October.
“My guess will be as soon as his elections are over, you’re going to see a plane full of Canadian negotiators flying down,” he said.
“We’re just being used by them. That’s what happened. That’s why it ended. It didn’t happen for math. The math was sensational.”
With a report from Irene Galea in Washington

sources.news_title: Canada's Mark Carney fires back after Trump renames Lake Ontario: "America is changing"
sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” for U.S. government use, the latest escalation in a growing dispute with Canada over trade. The executive order has since sparked a response from Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who highlighted that the name is over 400 years old and said, "America is changing."
The order updates the lake’s name in the U.S. geographic naming system, but Canada is not required to adopt the change and has given no indication it will.
Trump signed the order in the Oval Office, where a display map of the Great Lakes behind him showed “Lake America” printed in large red letters over Lake Ontario. Speaking to reporters, the president criticized Canada’s approach to trade, calling it difficult to deal with and accusing the country of feeling “entitled.”
The move echoes Trump's earlier effort to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America," another attempt to rebrand a prominent geographic feature through executive action.
“So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean,” Trump said. “So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them.”
Newsweek has reached out to Carney, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and New York Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul via email on Thursday afternoon for comment.
Carney reacted to the move, saying on X on Thursday in part, "We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always."
Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote on X, "It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever."
The executive order follows days of public remarks in which Trump suggested the name change after U.S.-Canada trade talks broke down. The administration recently announced 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, deepening tensions between the two longtime allies.
Canada responded with tariffs of its own on $20 billion in U.S. goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment.
Trump has also repeatedly taunted Canada since returning to office, including by suggesting it should become the 51st U.S. state.
Patrick Brown, mayor of Brampton, Ontario, told CNN Thursday afternoon, "We're still going to call it Lake Ontario."
"The only person who is having trouble with what to call it is your president. The whole notion is a bit preposterous. And just like if our prime minister wanted to rename the Mississippi (River), you'd probably get a chuckle out of it. It is having the same reaction in Canada."
Hochul wrote Thursday on X, frankly, "New York won’t be calling it that."
Scott Jennings, former adviser to ex-President George W. Bush, called Trump's move a "troll" on CNN Thursday night. "I'm more interested in actually what happens with Canada," he added. "They need us more than we need them and it's absolutely true that Canada has been treating many U.S. industries and U.S. workers very poorly and very unfairly for a long time."
Jennings also said he likes the "tough negotiations."
Where Is Lake Ontario?
Lake Ontario, which covers about 7,340 square miles, is the smallest of the five Great Lakes shared by the United States and Canada. The lake, roughly the size of New Jersey, forms part of the international border, separating New York state from Ontario, Canada’s most populous province and home to Toronto, the country’s largest city.
Ontario is also a major trading partner for numerous U.S. states, underscoring the region's economic significance at the center of the latest political dispute.
Lake Ontario's name traces its roots to the Huron Indigenous people's word oniatarí:io, meaning "lake of shining waters." The lake later lent its name to Ontario when it was established in 1867.
"It is quite possible that Canadians could see the appropriation of Lake Ontario and its renaming as part of the larger effort on the part of the U.S. to exert its influence territorially," Derek Alderman, a cultural and historical geographer, told Newsweek. He added that the move seemed intended "to exert some advantage or strength in the trade war with Canada."
Meanwhile, Reuben Rose-Redwood, professor of geography at the University of Victoria, called it "pure rage bait" and a "well-worn move from the Trump playbook akin to calling Canada the '51st State' or renaming the Gulf of Mexico to capture media attention."
“Trump’s threat to rename Lake Ontario is pure rage bait aimed at stoking anger among Canadians while distracting Americans from the fact that Trump overplayed his hand in the trade negotiations with Canada," he told Newsweek.
Who Owns Lake Ontario?
No single country "owns" Lake Ontario. The lake is shared by the United States and Canada, with the international border running through the water. Canada borders the lake to the north through the province of Ontario, while New York State lies along its southern shore. Jurisdiction over the lake is divided between the two countries under a series of treaties and agreements governing navigation, environmental protection, fishing and water management.
How Donald Trump Can Legally Rename Lake Ontario
Trump can direct the federal government to use a different name for Lake Ontario through an executive order for U.S. government purposes. Such an order allows federal agencies and mapping systems under U.S. authority to adopt the new designation. However, the president cannot compel Canada, foreign governments or international organizations to recognize the change.

US President Donald Trump on Thursday signed an executive order directing the US government to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America,” escalating an increasingly bitter dispute with Canada. The change is set to take effect immediately.
Trump had threatened Lake Ontario name change
Trump first raised the idea on Tuesday (August 25), saying the United States was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name because Washington did not expect to be doing much business with Ontario. His proposal came as trade negotiations between the US and Canada broke down.
The move follows Trump's earlier effort to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”, which similarly directed US federal agencies to use the new name.
Trump issued the order on the Gulf name change after returning to office, directing US federal agencies to use the new designation. As with the latest move involving Lake Ontario, the US government can adopt the name for its own official purposes but cannot force other countries or international organisations to follow suit.
Trump suggested that his campaign to rename major bodies of water may not end with Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico.
“So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean,” Trump told reporters.
“Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them,” he added.
Where is Lake Ontario?
Lake Ontario straddles the US-Canada border, with New York State on its southern shore and Canada's Ontario province to the north. Its shared status makes any unilateral US renaming largely a matter of how American government agencies refer to the lake.
Name change comes amid escalating trade tensions
Trump's decision comes as the US and Canada remain locked in a major trade dispute.
Canada announced that it would impose tariffs on about $20 billion worth of US imports, with the measures set to take effect on September 8. The duties target hundreds of products and match Washington's latest tariffs dollar-for-dollar.

sources.text:
Trump order renames Lake Ontario to Lake America
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Aug. 27 renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America in a move that he said takes effect immediately.
The change is a presidential snub to Canada amid an escalating trade war with the United States' northern neighbor and second-largest trading partner; however, Trump claimed in remarks in the Oval Office that he wasn't trying to send any messages to Canada.
"Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly. Even the military. We defend Canada for nothing. We don't get anything. They don't pay us to defend Canada," Trump said.
"They want to be treated like they're a state, and so we just can't do that anymore. ... The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They're nasty people."
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in response that the name Lake Ontario would endure "then, now and always," saying the name comes the Wendat word "Ontari’io" that "appropriately, means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”
"The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America," Carney said on X.com.
"We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario ― then, now and always."
The lake renaming comes after Trump's new 50% tariffs took effect on about 5% of imports from Canada after trade talks collapsed last week, with Canada over the weekend retaliating with "dollar for dollar" tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on $20 billion worth of U.S. imports.
Trump's executive order claims that the United States is the "greatest protector" of the Great Lakes, including Lake Ontario.
Without the security and investment that the U.S. provides, according to the order, the lakes would not be open for shipping or recreation to the extent they are today, noting nearly $4 billion invested by the U.S. in protecting the lakes' ecosystem over the last decade. The order says Canada invested "far less" in similar efforts over the same period.
The formal order also says the deepest parts of Lake Ontario’s waters sit within United States territory and that the U.S. claims most of the lake’s water volume. Within 30 days, the Secretary of the Interior is supposed to "take all appropriate actions to rename as 'Lake America' the body of water currently named as Lake Ontario."
Trump said the lake name change was something he'd thought about "for a long time" and that maybe he would also rename the Atlantic or Pacific oceans.
"We have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean," Trump said.
The order states that U.S. federal government references to Lake Ontario, including on executive department and agency maps, contracts and other documents and communications, are also to reflect the renaming. Other countries don't have to recognize the change.
The name “Ontario” is an Anglican pronunciation of an Iroquois word that means something like “shining sea” or “beautiful lake,” said Daniel Macfarlane, a professor at Western Michigan University’s School of Environment, Geography and Sustainability and author of “The Lives of Lake Ontario.”
That means the name of the lake predates European settlers or the founding of both the United States and Canada. French settlers tried to rename the lake to Lac de St. Louis or Lac Frontenac, but those monikers didn’t stick, Macfarlane said. Ontario won out.
The province of Ontario was named after the lake, Macfarlane said.
“Calling it Lake America is kind of ridiculous,” he said. “It’s ridiculous, ludicrous for other reasons. … It’s far more a Canadian lake and far more important to Canada than it is to the U.S.”
A quarter of Canadians live within the Lake Ontario watershed, whereas the U.S. share of Lake Ontario watershed is “back woods” without a major city, Macfarlane said. The lake is integral to the Toronto economy, a major Canadian population center on the lakeshore.
“Canada would not have become a separate country from the U.S. if not for Lake Ontario,” Macfarlane said. “It serves as both a bridge and a barrier between the two countries.”
Macfarlane questioned whether Trump can rename Lake Ontario as part of his campaign to pressure the Canadians back to the negotiating table on trade.
"Canada's not going to recognize it," he said. "They have no way to compel Canada to recognize it. The rest of the world's not going to recognize it. It's just like the Gulf of America."
Last year, Trump issued an order to rename the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America on the first day of his second term.
Lake America 'shenanigans'
Canada’s minister of industry on Aug. 26 also rejected Trump’s idea to change the name of Lake Ontario.
"We’ll always call it Lake Ontario. Period," Mélanie Joly said in response to a reporter’s question about Trump’s proposal.
"We’re proud of our Great Lakes," Joly added about the indigenous name for the lake. "We’ve navigated the St. Lawrence River ― the Great Lakes ― for thousands of years, and it was part of the foundation of our country. We’ll just stand up for what we have.
"Meanwhile, I really think that, while all these shenanigans are happening, we'll just be smart, we'll be strategic and we'll fight back," she added.
Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who is the Democratic nominee for Michigan governor, said Thursday that renaming a lake won't lower a grocery bill, put more money in people’s pockets or bring back supplier contracts that Michigan companies just lost.
“While the President is workshopping map graphics, Michiganders are staring down a 50% tariff raising costs on steel and the cars we build here, and Ontario is threatening the electricity that keeps the lights on for 1.5 million Americans," Benson said in a statement.
"Canada is our closest ally and our biggest customer. Treating them like an enemy is a gift to China, and Michigan pays for it.”
A spokesman for Gov. Gretchen Whitmer said Thursday that the renaming is a distraction from what truly matters.
"The fact is our relationship with Canada supports hundreds of thousands of jobs on both sides of the border. The governor's concern right now is the 50% tariff on autos and steel, which will make things more expensive for Michiganders and lead to layoffs," Whitmer spokesman Bobby Leddy said.
"Tariffs are a tax on Michigan families, and no name change fixes that. We should be sitting down with Canada, not picking fights with them.”
U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell, an Ann Arbor Democrat, said Trump "can sign all the executive orders he wants, but it will always be Lake Ontario."
"Canada is not our enemy. It is our neighbor, our ally, and one of Michigan’s most important economic partners. It is a friendship that no stroke of a pen can erase,” Dingell said.
Trump also has repeatedly floated making Canada the 51st state, though Canadian officials have flatly rejected that.
Lake Ontario is the only one of the five Great Lakes that doesn't border Michigan. The lake runs along western New York State on the U.S. side and serves as an important shipping route to the Atlantic Ocean. Toronto sits on Lake Ontario on the Canadian side.
Scholars said the name Ontario comes from the Huron tribe's word for “lake of shining water,” or in Iroquois it means "beautiful lake." The lake was also called Lake St. Louis by explorer Samuel de Champlain in 1632, according to Michigan State University. The smallest of the Great Lakes, its surface area covers about 7,340 square miles.
USA Today contributed.

sources.text:
Trump signs order to change Lake Ontario into ‘Lake America’ as his fight with Canada spirals
Trump’s order has no effect outside the United States
President Donald Trump signed an order to rename one of the five Great Lakes along the U.S.-Canada border in a fit of rage over his ongoing trade war with Ottawa that appears to have no end in sight.
On Thursday, Trump signed an order directing federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America” in all official documents and records, echoing a similar move from early in his second term when he attempted to unilaterally rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.”
While the president does have the authority to direct how the government recognizes the names of places and landmarks, he cannot force Canada or individual citizens on either side of the border to follow his preferred naming conventions.
The move, intended as a branch to a flagging political base that has grown increasingly disenchanted with his presidency and his administration’s failure to address the cost of living concerns that drove them to vote for him nearly two years ago, comes as Trump continues to antagonize traditional American allies for no apparent reason other than his own deeply-ingrained belief that the country has somehow been disrespected by allies who act as sovereign states rather than vassals.
Speaking in the Oval Office as he signed the order, Trump suggested that the decision was in part motivated by displeasure over what he described as Ottawa’s failure to pay the United States mob-style “protection” money for the privilege of existing under the American military umbrella.
“You know, we defend Canada for nothing. We don't get anything. They don't pay us to defend Canada, but we defend Canada, and they understand that. As an example, we bought icebreakers. They'd like to use them. We have 11 brand new icebreakers coming in, they'd like to use the icebreakers. They don't pay for anything, and they want to be treated like a state, but they're not a state,” he said.
He added that the “whole Canadian thing” has been “going on for decades” and “has to stop” while offering up the example of automobile manufacturing as something that he believes should be entirely re-shored to the U.S.
Asked why he was antagonizing one of America’s traditional allies even as he continues to cozy up to dictators in China and North Korea, Trump lashed out at leaders in Ottawa for pushing back against his trade war with retaliatory tariffs that they levied in response to the ones he ordered after trade talks broke down last week.
“The Canadian officials have treated us very badly — they’re nasty people,” he said.
Trump then suggested that Canada was “the worst to deal with on trade” despite the country’s long relationship with the U.S. and the trade agreement his administration negotiated during his first term.
He complained that Canadians “feel entitled” and added that “we can’t have that.”
Trump had teased the troll-ish renaming order in a video posted to TikTok earlier this week.
In the video, he displayed a map of the Great Lakes and suggested he would do exactly what he did on Thursday.
“We’re gonna make a little change; we’re gonna call it something different than Lake Ontario,” the 80-year-old president said. “We’re gonna call it Lake America. And all it takes is a good pen and some intelligence.”
Trump, a former real estate mogul with a penchant for branding, then used a Sharpie to cross out the lake’s name and write “LAKE AMERICA” above it.
His geographic broadside at America’s northern neighbor is the latest episode in a series of events that have fractured the relationship between the two countries.
According to The Globe and Mail, Canadian defense forces have begun modeling a response to a hypothetical U.S. invasion for the first time in more than a century.
Since taking office last January, Trump has repeatedly expressed his desire to acquire Canada, which he described on multiple occasions as “the 51st state.” And in recent weeks, he’s reportedly turned his attention back to Canada, fixating on the country’s “vulnerability” to foreign adversaries in its Arctic reaches.
At the same time, the 80-year-old president has made clear his desire to take control of Greenland, a territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, another NATO ally. The White House, which says it needs Greenland for purposes of national security, sees several options to achieve this goal, including the use of military force.

WASHINGTON — President Trump signed documents Thursday ordering that Lake Ontario be renamed “Lake America” — as he and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney escalate their tariffs-driven trade war.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario, effective immediately, to Lake America,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
“We filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else. We notified all of the various people that we have to notify. So we’ve done everything that you have to do, and this is official, effective immediately.”
Trump said that “the Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people. They charge our farmers 400% tariffs.”
Trump previously renamed the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” last year.
“If you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” Trump said.
Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) said New York would be defying Trump’s wishes on renaming the lake that hugs its northern border.
“New York won’t be calling it that,” Hochul declared on X.
Carney also rejected the rebrand, saying that “the name is more than 400 years old” and “comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.’”
“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” he tweeted. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
The prime minister broke off trade talks with the US on Friday and claimed that “America is trying to break us so that they can own us,” but that so long as he was in charge it would “never, ever happen.”
Trump imposed a new 50% tariff Saturday on $20 billion of Canadian goods, including beer, cheese, wine, hockey sticks, cement and electronics.
He also threatened to hike tariffs to 50% on all vehicles, automotive parts and steel coming from Canada.
Carney vowed to fight back with retaliatory tariffs beginning on Sept. 8.
Canada’s population of 41 million is about 12% the size of the US and its economy is much smaller, meaning it would disproportionately feel the effect of a trade war.
More than 70% of Canada’s exports go to the US and about half of its imports come through its southern border.
The US is much less reliant on Canada, with about 14% of US exports going to Canada. Canadian goods amount to about 11.5% of overall American imports.
Vice President JD Vance visited Maine on Monday and hammered Carney.
“Canada is a country that has underinvested in its military that quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States,” Vance said.
“Canada allows itself to be used as a backdoor for Chinese goods. They treat Chinese goods more fairly than they do [those] that come from the people of Maine.”

Susan Collins (R-Maine) told News Center Maine. “If it comes back with a huge tariff on it, perhaps as much as 50 percent, that increases the cost of eating, building homes and merch[andising] our best-known products.”

"We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms," Carney wrote in an X post.
"Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always," he wrote.
The executive action marks the second time Trump has targeted the long-enduring name of an international body of water and renamed it for the U.S.
On the first day of his second term, Trump signed an order to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America." The attempt to rename the gulf, which has gone by the same name since the 16th Century, drew international opposition, and numerous media outlets vowed to stick with the common and internationally recognized usage.
Trump said Thursday, "If you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic, and/or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both."
When asked what message he was trying to send by renaming Lake Ontario, Trump initially claimed, "No message."
But he immediately added, "Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade."
"They don't pay for anything, and they want to be treated like a state, but they're not a state," Trump said. Last year, he angered many Canadians by repeatedly advocating for making their country the 51st U.S. state.
The latest provocation could further inflame tensions between the U.S. and Canada, whose trade war reignited over the weekend when Trump imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.
Canada responded by announcing "dollar for dollar" retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% on imports from the U.S., currently set to take effect on Sept. 8.
On Wednesday evening, Canada said it would pare back some of those tariffs targeting seafood and fish products "to protect against broader economic harms."
But the new round of import taxes could still raise costs and reduce choices for consumers, as Carney acknowledged after the two countries' trade negotiations fell apart Friday evening.
But Trump, an ardent fan of tariffs who has long complained about the U.S. maintaining trade deficits with its economic partners, dismissed the idea that the dispute could exacerbate affordability in the U.S.
"Ultimately, it's going to be very good for us," Trump said Thursday afternoon, citing the average annual U.S. trade deficit with Canada.
"It's too much. We can't lose that. We don't want to lose that. We don't want to lose it anymore," he said.
Lake Ontario's centuries-old name comes from the Iroquoian word "oniatarí:io," meaning "lake of shining waters," according to the Center for Great Lakes Literacy.
It is farthest east of the five Great Lakes, the world's largest freshwater system. It is bordered to the north by the Canadian province of Ontario and to the south by New York.
Trump's move drew derision from some of his Democratic critics.
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker mockingly wrote on X that Chicago's Trump Tower "is renamed to NATALIE TOWER," referencing a recent controversy surrounding presidential aide Natalie Harp.
Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers responded to Trump's action by posting a video of himself at a McDonald's signing a napkin labeled "Lake Wisconsin."
"And I just renamed Lake Michigan Lake Wisconsin," Evers wrote in the X post. "See, I can sign napkins that say things, too."
